options.D: Invention without innovation (commercialization/adoption missing)

2yr-13.stem: A fast follower launches after a rival’s success with minor tweaks. In the Four I’s, this is mainly:

options.A: Imitation of a proven commercialization template
options.B: Idea because it is conceptual repositioning
options.C: Innovation because followers are always “new to world”
options.D: Invention because entry transforms copies into novelty

2yr-13.stem: A firm increases R&D but reduces market experimentation. Under speed-of-innovation logic, this likely:

options.A: Slows learning because feedback cycles lengthen
options.B: Speeds learning because labs replace customers
options.C: Eliminates imitation because customers see less
options.D: Guarantees radical innovation by spending more

2yr-13.stem: A firm patents a recommendation model. The Chapter 7–consistent risk is:

options.A: Disclosure helps rivals learn, eroding advantage
options.B: Patents remove substitutes from the category
options.C: Patents force adoption by lowering buyer risk
options.D: Disclosure prevents rivals learning, preserving secrecy

2yr-13.stem: A firm expects imitation after success. The best sustaining response is:

options.A: Publish details because disclosure slows competitors
options.B: Outsource learning to raise inimitability
options.C: Build complements and continuously innovate beyond the visible feature
options.D: Switch to pipeline because platforms are always copied

2yr-13.stem: A press release announces a “revolutionary” concept without a working artifact. The correct label is:

options.A: Imitation because all concepts copy prior work
options.B: Idea, not invention or innovation yet
options.C: Invention because announcing makes it real
options.D: Innovation because communication equals commercialization

2yr-13.stem: Patent expiry followed by entry fits which story best?

options.A: Temporary monopoly until imitation/entry accelerates
options.B: Permanent monopoly because patents never end
options.C: Consumer surplus replacing producer capture by definition
options.D: Platform rents replacing patent rents automatically

2yr-13.stem: A startup says “imitation proves we are losing.” Chapter 7 implies instead:

options.A: Imitation often follows success; the issue becomes renewal
options.B: Imitation occurs only after failure, not success
options.C: Imitation occurs only in maturity, not early stages
options.D: Imitation is impossible in software markets

2yr-13.stem: A firm stalls because rivals iterate faster after initial adoption. Best diagnosis is:

options.A: Patents are too broad, reducing customer adoption
options.B: Network effects prevent improvement incentives
options.C: Cadence too slow for accelerating change; learning falls behind
options.D: Radical innovation must never be improved incrementally

2yr-13.stem: The Four I’s sequence is best captured as:

options.A: Idea → Invention → Innovation → Imitation
options.B: Innovation → Imitation → Invention → Idea
options.C: Idea → Innovation → Invention → Imitation
options.D: Invention → Idea → Imitation → Innovation

2yr-13.stem: The most discriminating test between “invention” and “innovation” is whether:

options.A: It uses new technology internally
options.B: Scientists agree it is publishable
options.C: Customers adopt it through commercialization at scale
options.D: It has a patent number assigned

2yr-13.stem: Apple Vision Pro’s early buyers were largely enthusiasts and early adopters. In chasm terms, the next major hurdle is convincing the:

options.A: Technology enthusiasts, who adopt after standards are entrenched and brands are well established
options.B: Laggards, who pay premium prices for beta products and tolerate high uncertainty in use
options.C: Late majority, who purchase first and then create reference cases for other segments to follow
options.D: Early majority, who demand reliability, clear use cases, standards, and strong support before adoption

2yr-13.stem: Tesla’s Model 3/Model Y are discussed as helping it cross the big chasm. The strategic logic is most directly:

options.A: Higher-priced models create exclusivity, pushing adoption from late majority toward early adopters
options.B: New patents prevent imitation, pushing adoption from laggards toward early enthusiasts immediately
options.C: Network effects guarantee adoption, pushing adoption from early majority toward early adopters over time
options.D: Lower-priced models broaden adoption from early adopters toward the early majority segment

2yr-13.stem: An EV startup wins early adopters but loses early majority because repairs take months and service is inconsistent. The best diagnosis is:

options.A: It failed the ‘whole product’ test, where pragmatists need dependable after-sales support and reliability
options.B: It failed the patent test, where pragmatists refuse products lacking legal exclusivity protections
options.C: It failed the novelty test, where pragmatists demand unproven experimental features more than reliability
options.D: It failed the price test, where pragmatists adopt only when prices rise and signal premium quality

2yr-13.stem: Generative AI copilots spread rapidly across teams, then adoption slows as firms demand governance and safety. This slowdown most resembles movement toward:

options.A: Laggard entry, where adoption happens only in decline stage and therefore requires forced compliance
options.B: Technology enthusiast dominance, where beta instability is rewarded because experimentation is the main objective
options.C: Early majority concerns, where standards, integration, and risk controls become prerequisites for broad adoption
options.D: Decline stage, where market contraction is dominant and new adoption is structurally impossible

2yr-13.stem: A micro-mobility industry saw rapid entry and then many exits in several cities. This pattern most closely signals:

options.A: Shakeout stage dynamics, where rivalry intensifies, weaker firms exit, and consolidation accelerates
options.B: Maturity stage expansion, where entrants proliferate and product variety grows without consolidation
options.C: Introduction stage stability, where uncertainty drops and competitors converge without exits
options.D: Decline stage completion, where demand collapses to near zero and no replacement cycles remain

2yr-13.stem: A wearable category is still searching for a dominant design and has uncertain standards. The most consistent life-cycle stage is:

options.A: Shakeout stage, where dominant design is fully settled and entry accelerates without exits
options.B: Introduction stage, where uncertainty is high and designs compete before a dominant design emerges
options.C: Maturity stage, where standards are entrenched and incremental efficiency becomes the main driver
options.D: Decline stage, where the market contracts and firms harvest rather than invest in new designs

2yr-13.stem: A smartphone market is replacement-driven with slower growth and intense price competition. The best stage label is:

options.A: Growth stage, where first-time adoption dominates and differentiation expands variety without pressure
options.B: Introduction stage, where uncertainty is highest and standards have not emerged across producers
options.C: Maturity stage, where replacement demand rises and rivalry focuses on efficiency and pricing
options.D: Decline stage, where adoption becomes unnecessary and firms should exit immediately and harvest cash

2yr-13.stem: A SaaS startup wants to cross the chasm in one vertical before expanding broadly. This is aligned with:

options.A: Laggard-first strategy because laggards are the biggest market and adopt reliably without support
options.B: Horizontal strategy to enter all verticals first so early majority can pick any configuration needed
options.C: Decline-stage strategy because chasm crossing is easiest once an industry begins shrinking structurally
options.D: Beachhead strategy to win one niche with references and whole-product completeness, then expand adjacently

2yr-13.stem: A new consumer device market shows explosive demand growth and many entrants, but standards begin to stabilize. This best fits:

options.A: Decline stage, where demand falls structurally and firms should harvest rather than invest
options.B: Growth stage, where adoption accelerates and entry intensifies while standards start to clarify
options.C: Shakeout stage, where exits dominate because growth has ended and consolidation is underway
options.D: Maturity stage, where replacement dominates and innovation becomes mostly incremental efficiency

2yr-13.stem: A firm tries to cross the chasm by adding features while reliability and support remain weak. The most likely outcome is:

options.A: It fails only if patents expire because chasm crossing is mainly a legal exclusivity problem
options.B: It still fails because early majority values risk reduction and whole-product support over feature novelty
options.C: It succeeds because features substitute fully for standards, references, and after-sales support
options.D: It succeeds because pragmatists adopt first and prefer novelty even when service is unreliable

2yr-13.stem: A fintech category sees rapid adoption, strong new user growth, and many entrants adding capacity. Stage inference is:

options.A: Growth stage, where adoption accelerates and entry intensifies as firms pursue scale and position
options.B: Maturity stage, where replacement dominates and firms compete mainly on incremental efficiency
options.C: Shakeout stage, where exits dominate because consolidation has already reduced competitors
options.D: Decline stage, where demand falls structurally and new entrants avoid the market entirely

2yr-13.stem: A market shows intense consolidation, exits, and a few surviving leaders around a dominant design. Stage inference is:

options.A: Growth stage, where entry is high and exits are low because demand is exploding everywhere
options.B: Decline stage, where demand is near zero and firms cannot profitably sell any units
options.C: Introduction stage, where uncertainty falls and designs become more diverse with stable entry
options.D: Shakeout stage, where rivalry rises and weaker firms exit as the industry consolidates

2yr-13.stem: A product is adopted only when necessary and buyers avoid new technology for personal or economic reasons. This describes:

options.A: Laggards, who enter late and adopt only when adoption becomes unavoidable in practice
options.B: Early majority, who adopt early and tolerate uncertainty because novelty is intrinsically valued
options.C: Technology enthusiasts, who wait for entrenched standards and strong brands before buying
options.D: Early adopters, who pay premiums for beta products to signal status and experiment

2yr-13.stem: Late majority is similar to early majority but more risk-averse. The most correct statement is:

options.A: Late majority is identical to laggards, so both segments should be pursued aggressively for growth
options.B: Late majority buys mainly for novelty, making standards and support far less important than features
options.C: Late majority is similar to early majority but more risk-averse and more brand-dependent in adoption
options.D: Late majority is less risk-averse than early adopters and therefore buys unfinished beta designs first

2yr-13.stem: A market shows saturation, slower growth, and competition shifting to incremental improvements and efficiency. Stage inference is:

options.A: Maturity stage, where growth slows and firms compete through efficiency and incremental innovation
options.B: Growth stage, where adoption accelerates and variety expands faster than efficiency pressures
options.C: Introduction stage, where uncertainty is highest and designs compete before standards emerge
options.D: Shakeout stage, where exits dominate and only a few firms remain after consolidation

2yr-13.stem: Smartphones are in growth in many emerging economies and in maturity in developed economies. The clearest implication is:

options.A: The industry life cycle is invalid because a product cannot be in two stages at the same time
options.B: The shakeout stage is irrelevant because digital goods do not experience consolidation dynamics
options.C: The same firm may need different strategies across geographies because life-cycle stage differs by market
options.D: The decline stage must be next everywhere because maturity in one market forces global contraction

2yr-13.stem: A company markets heavily to late majority before fixing early majority concerns. Most likely result:

options.A: Weak adoption only if patents exist, because patents make late-majority buyers suspicious
options.B: Weak adoption, because late majority waits for entrenched standards and strong brands built via early majority momentum
options.C: Strong adoption, because late majority buys without references, standards, or support
options.D: Strong adoption, because late majority values beta testing and tolerates imperfections most

2yr-13.stem: The largest “chasm” is typically between:

options.A: Early adopters and early majority
options.B: Technology enthusiasts and laggards
options.C: Early majority and laggards
options.D: Late majority and laggards

2yr-13.stem: A market shows dominant design, intense rivalry, and exits. Best stage label:

options.A: Decline
options.B: Shakeout
options.C: Introduction
options.D: Growth

2yr-13.stem: In decline, the most coherent general move is often:

options.A: Harvest or niche-focus rather than broad expansion
options.B: Build capacity aggressively for scale
options.C: Ignore cash flows and reinvest heavily
options.D: Maximize variety and experimentation

2yr-13.stem: A “whole product” emphasis means:

options.A: Core product alone with maximum features
options.B: Price cuts alone with no service investment
options.C: Core product plus complements, support, reliability, and standards
options.D: Patent portfolio plus PR campaigns

2yr-13.stem: A firm in growth should typically prioritize:

options.A: Harvesting cash immediately
options.B: Scaling while learning and positioning before consolidation arrives
options.C: Exiting early to avoid rivalry
options.D: Eliminating variety to enforce standards

2yr-13.stem: A firm in introduction stage should typically prioritize:

options.A: Consolidating competitors
options.B: Learning fast and finding product–market fit under uncertainty
options.C: Locking standards through scale manufacturing
options.D: Harvesting stable cash flows

2yr-13.stem: In maturity, competitive advantage often shifts toward:

options.A: Ignoring customer support and complements
options.B: Radical category creation only
options.C: Pure monopoly pricing without value improvements
options.D: Incremental innovation and efficiency improvements

2yr-13.stem: A chasm-crossing “beachhead” is mainly used to:

options.A: Create credible references and reduce risk for pragmatists
options.B: Target laggards for predictable first adoption
options.C: Avoid learning and delay commercialization
options.D: Eliminate substitutes through patents

2yr-13.stem: Amazon improves Alexa with better speech recognition using existing ML methods for existing customers. In Exhibit 7.12 terms, this is:

options.A: Architectural innovation, creating a new market using existing technologies with no change in use
options.B: Incremental innovation, improving an existing offering for existing markets using existing technologies
options.C: Disruptive innovation, entering a new fringe market and later moving upmarket to displace incumbents
options.D: Radical innovation, creating a new market using new technologies that replace prior knowledge bases

2yr-13.stem: A new gene-editing therapy creates a new category and new market applications. In Exhibit 7.12, it best fits:

options.A: Radical innovation, targeting new markets by using new technologies from novel knowledge bases
options.B: Disruptive innovation, starting low-end in existing markets and then improving to match incumbents
options.C: Architectural innovation, targeting new markets using existing technologies without new science
options.D: Incremental innovation, improving existing offerings for existing markets using existing technologies

2yr-13.stem: A cheaper, initially inferior product starts in a fringe segment and later improves to threaten incumbents. The closest label is:

options.A: Incremental innovation, improving existing offerings but never threatening incumbent business models
options.B: Radical innovation, beginning as premium performance and targeting mainstream customers from day one
options.C: Disruptive innovation, entering from fringe markets and moving upmarket over time to challenge leaders
options.D: Architectural innovation, applying new technology in existing markets without changing market trajectories

2yr-13.stem: A startup uses existing payment rails but targets newly served segments in a new market. Exhibit 7.12 suggests:

options.A: Incremental innovation, improving existing offerings for existing markets using the same technology
options.B: Architectural innovation, using existing technologies to create or serve a new market space
options.C: Disruptive innovation, requiring inferior quality and low price as a necessary condition always
options.D: Radical innovation, requiring new technologies whenever a new segment is targeted at all

2yr-13.stem: A company builds a new chip architecture but sells it to existing data-center customers. Exhibit 7.12 implies:

options.A: Disruptive innovation, because new chips must start low-end and then move up to mainstream buyers
options.B: Architectural innovation, applying a new technology configuration to an existing market space
options.C: Incremental innovation, because semiconductors only improve steadily without discontinuity by definition
options.D: Radical innovation, because any new technology implies a new market regardless of customer base

2yr-13.stem: A smartphone maker upgrades camera software and battery management using the same chip platform for current users. Exhibit 7.12 label is:

options.A: Radical innovation, creating new markets because any improvement creates a new category of buyers
options.B: Disruptive innovation, starting low-end and then moving upmarket as incumbents overshoot demand
options.C: Incremental innovation, improving existing products in existing markets using existing technologies
options.D: Architectural innovation, creating new markets using existing technologies without altering the product

2yr-13.stem: A product based on new materials and methods targets a new application market. Exhibit 7.12 label is:

options.A: Architectural innovation, using existing technologies to create a new market without new knowledge
options.B: Disruptive innovation, entering existing markets at premium tiers and then moving downmarket
options.C: Incremental innovation, improving existing products for existing markets with existing technologies
options.D: Radical innovation, combining new technologies with new markets and sometimes creating new industries

2yr-13.stem: A firm reconfigures existing components into a new system architecture for its current customer base without new science. The closest label is:

options.A: Radical innovation, because recombination always implies a new market and a new technology knowledge base
options.B: Incremental innovation, because it recombines existing knowledge for existing markets without new technology bases
options.C: Architectural innovation, because any internal redesign necessarily creates a new market by definition
options.D: Disruptive innovation, because system redesigns always begin low-end and then displace premium incumbents

2yr-13.stem: A premium, higher-performance product is called “disruptive.” The best critique is:

options.A: That pattern is radical by definition, because premium implies new market creation automatically
options.B: That pattern is architectural by definition, because premium products always target existing markets
options.C: That pattern is disruptive by definition, because disruption equals superior performance at launch
options.D: That pattern resembles sustaining improvement; disruption typically enters fringe or new markets first

2yr-13.stem: Existing tech + existing market improvements generally classify as:

options.A: Radical
options.B: Architectural
options.C: Disruptive
options.D: Incremental

2yr-13.stem: New tech + new market creation generally classify as:

options.A: Incremental
options.B: Architectural
options.C: Radical
options.D: Disruptive

2yr-13.stem: New tech + existing market generally classify as:

options.A: Architectural
options.B: Radical
options.C: Incremental
options.D: Disruptive

2yr-13.stem: Existing tech + new market generally classify as:

options.A: Disruptive
options.B: Incremental
options.C: Architectural
options.D: Radical

2yr-13.stem: “Most innovations are radical.” The best correction is:

options.A: Most innovations are radical because markets demand novelty
options.B: Most innovations are architectural only
options.C: Most innovations are incremental, despite attention to breakthroughs
options.D: Most innovations are disruptive, not incremental

2yr-13.stem: “New to our firm” does not necessarily mean “radical.” The correct diagnostic is:

options.A: Founder charisma and early funding size
options.B: Marketing excitement and press coverage intensity
options.C: Patent status and court enforceability
options.D: Newness to market and technology axes, not internal novelty

2yr-13.stem: A firm’s radical breakthrough is followed by many small upgrades. The best interpretation is:

options.A: Radical creates lead; incremental sustains advantage over time
options.B: Disruption requires only one upgrade cycle
options.C: Radical makes incremental illegal
options.D: Incremental makes radical impossible

2yr-13.stem: Disruptive innovation is best described as:

options.A: New technology plus new market always
options.B: Entry via fringe/new markets with different attributes, then upmarket movement
options.C: Existing technology plus existing market always
options.D: Immediate domination of mainstream markets through superior premium performance

2yr-13.stem: A firm recombines existing modules for a better experience without new science in the same market. Best label is:

options.A: Incremental innovation
options.B: Radical innovation
options.C: Architectural innovation
options.D: Disruptive innovation

2yr-13.stem: A firm uses new tech to sell to existing customers. That is most consistent with:

options.A: Architectural innovation
options.B: Disruptive innovation
options.C: Incremental innovation
options.D: Radical innovation

2yr-13.stem: A firm uses existing tech to reach customers previously outside the category. That is most consistent with:

options.A: Radical innovation
options.B: Incremental innovation
options.C: Disruptive innovation
options.D: Architectural innovation

2yr-13.stem: The diagonal pairing in the framework highlights:

options.A: Radical vs disruptive only
options.B: Incremental vs architectural only
options.C: Incremental vs radical, and architectural vs disruptive
options.D: Disruptive vs incremental only

2yr-13.stem: The most diagnostic question for classification is:

options.A: Legal disputes and patent filings
options.B: Existing vs new markets, and existing vs new technologies
options.C: Influencer engagement and brand mentions
options.D: Profit margin changes in the first quarter

2yr-13.stem: A firm sells a premium product that improves mainstream performance and calls it disruptive. Best critique is:

options.A: Definitely disruptive because premium implies new market
options.B: Definitely disruptive because better performance defines disruption
options.C: Likely sustaining improvement, not classic disruption trajectory
options.D: Not classifiable because disruption depends only on patents

2yr-13.stem: An IoT cyber-physical system linking devices and analytics is most associated with:

options.A: The third industrial revolution driven by computers but not connected cyber-physical systems
options.B: The first industrial revolution driven by steam power and mechanization
options.C: The fourth industrial revolution with AI, automation, robotics, and IoT cyber-physical systems
options.D: The second industrial revolution driven by electrification and mass production

2yr-13.stem: Fourth industrial revolution dynamics are most likely to increase returns to:

options.A: Inventory stockpiles, because scarcity becomes the main source of advantage
options.B: Education and adaptable human capital, because routine tasks are more automatable
options.C: Corporate secrecy, because diffusion becomes impossible once automation expands
options.D: Retail floor space, because foot traffic is the central moat in cyber-physical markets

2yr-13.stem: Uber’s ride-hailing model is best classified as:

options.A: Incremental: cannot change industry economics
options.B: Pipeline: owns production and sells linearly
options.C: Radical: new tech plus new market by definition
options.D: Platform: matches external producers and consumers

2yr-13.stem: A rider becomes a driver within the same platform. This is:

options.A: Multi-homing
options.B: Side switching
options.C: Chasm crossing
options.D: Architectural innovation

2yr-13.stem: Airbnb scales supply without owning hotels mainly because it:

options.A: Crosses the chasm by targeting laggards first
options.B: Vertically integrates real estate to lower costs
options.C: Eliminates the need for governance because trust is automatic
options.D: Unlocks external supply through hosts in an asset-light manner

2yr-13.stem: Fraud/spam drives users away on a marketplace. The key platform lesson is:

options.A: Governance sustains trust; weak rules can collapse network effects
options.B: Governance matters only for pipelines with inventory
options.C: Governance is irrelevant; network effects are mechanical
options.D: Governance always hurts adoption; remove rules immediately

2yr-13.stem: More merchants accept a card network → more consumers carry it → more merchants join. This is:

options.A: Decline-stage replacement demand
options.B: Economies of scale only
options.C: Cross-side network effects
options.D: Radical innovation automatically

2yr-13.stem: “We are a platform” but the firm owns inventory, sets prices, and sells directly. Best diagnosis:

options.A: Radical innovation because inventory implies novelty
options.B: Social entrepreneurship because intermediation helps society
options.C: Mostly pipeline with digital distribution
options.D: True platform because any app is multi-sided

2yr-13.stem: Chicken-or-egg problem at launch is best solved by:

options.A: Raising fees early to signal quality
options.B: Seeding/subsidizing one side to create early transactions
options.C: Removing all rules to maximize entry
options.D: Waiting until both sides are naturally large

2yr-13.stem: A platform raises take rates aggressively before stabilizing network effects. Risk is:

options.A: Rivals exit because fees signal quality
options.B: Participation drops and network effects weaken
options.C: Chasm becomes irrelevant because fees imply reliability
options.D: Substitutes vanish because users lock in

2yr-13.stem: A platform opens APIs for complements but fails to enforce quality rules. Primary risk is:

options.A: Complements matter only in late majority stage
options.B: Patents prevent low-quality participants from joining
options.C: Trust collapses; participation falls; network effects weaken
options.D: Trust increases automatically through openness

2yr-13.stem: Strategic entrepreneurship is best described as:

options.A: Harvesting declining markets as a startup default
options.B: Copying incumbents only to reduce novelty risk
options.C: Doing philanthropy first and revenue later
options.D: Using strategy tools to build ventures that create and capture value

2yr-13.stem: Social entrepreneurship (as used here) is best described as:

options.A: Platform-only strategy because networks create all social value
options.B: Radical-only innovation because incremental cannot help society
options.C: Maximizing profit only and treating impact as externality
options.D: Pursuing social goals via ventures using triple-bottom-line performance

2yr-13.stem: A platform competitor copies the interface but lacks users. Why does it matter?

options.A: Advertising alone creates value; user counts are irrelevant
options.B: Without critical mass, network effects are weak and value is lower
options.C: Inventory ownership is the key; users are secondary
options.D: Interface copying is illegal so users automatically migrate

2yr-13.stem: “Platforms always outperform pipelines.” Best caveat is:

options.A: True only in decline stage, not in growth stage
options.B: True only with radical technology, not business design
options.C: Only if positive network effects and governance are achieved
options.D: Always true by definition, regardless of execution

2yr-13.stem: A platform’s “product” includes:

options.A: Only the HR hiring system
options.B: Only the user interface and brand slogan
options.C: Rules, trust mechanisms, incentives, and matching infrastructure
options.D: Only the financing structure and capital policy

2yr-13.stem: Multi-homing best describes:

options.A: A participant using multiple platforms at the same time
options.B: A firm shifting from incremental to radical innovation
options.C: A participant switching from consumer to producer
options.D: A firm moving from introduction to maturity stage

2yr-13.stem: A platform restricts third-party producers “to stay in control.” Core risk is:

options.A: Chicken-or-egg disappears because restriction forces joining
options.B: Network effects strengthen because fewer producers increases value
options.C: Ecosystem growth slows; network effects fail to scale
options.D: Chasm crossing becomes automatic because closure signals reliability

2yr-13.stem: A platform’s feedback loops create advantage mainly by:

options.A: Replacing the need for supply-side growth
options.B: Making patents unnecessary for all industries
options.C: Improving match quality and reducing friction through data learning
options.D: Eliminating the need for governance and moderation

2yr-13.stem: A platform stagnates after trust scandals. Best explanation is:

options.A: Trust scandals push adoption to late majority faster
options.B: Trust scandals reduce costs and improve margins
options.C: Trust scandals prove radical innovation is occurring
options.D: Reduced participation weakens network effects and value for remaining users

2yr-13.stem: A creator platform solves chicken-or-egg by guaranteeing buyers for first creators. This is:

options.A: Decline-stage repositioning
options.B: Harvesting demand in maturity stage
options.C: Architectural innovation classification
options.D: Seeding one side to create early proof and transactions

2yr-13.stem: A platform lowers take rate to attract more producers, expecting later growth. This is:

options.A: Subsidizing one side to ignite participation and network effects
options.B: Crossing the chasm by targeting laggards first
options.C: Converting invention into innovation automatically
options.D: Eliminating substitutes by predatory pricing

2yr-13.stem: A platform becomes valuable because more users join, not because unit costs fall. This is:

options.A: Economies of scale, not network effects
options.B: Life-cycle maturity, not platform dynamics
options.C: Network effects, not just economies of scale
options.D: Radical innovation, not platform dynamics

2yr-13.stem: A platform’s governance is best seen as:

options.A: A strategic lever shaping value creation and participation quality
options.B: A compliance detail unrelated to platform economics
options.C: A substitute for product design and customer experience
options.D: A late-stage activity only after maturity arrives

2yr-13.stem: A social enterprise earns revenue and also measures social outcomes. That fits best with:

options.A: Social entrepreneurship definition used in this chapter
options.B: Strategic entrepreneurship only
options.C: Pure imitation strategy
options.D: Decline-stage harvest strategy

2yr-13.stem: A platform adds complements through third parties. Most accurate implication is:

options.A: Governance becomes unnecessary because complements self-police
options.B: More value potential, but governance complexity rises sharply
options.C: Less value potential because complements always cannibalize
options.D: Network effects become irrelevant once complements exist

2yr-13.stem: Platform vs pipeline is best distinguished by whether the firm:

options.A: Is venture-funded or not
options.B: Operates globally or locally
options.C: Orchestrates interactions among external parties or owns production linearly
options.D: Uses technology or not

2yr-14.stem: Apple shifting from licensed Qualcomm modems to an in-house modem mainly changes which corporate strategy dimension?

options.A: Horizontal scope by entering unrelated product markets beyond device ecosystems.
options.B: Geographic scope by widening the countries where devices are sold and supported.
options.C: Business-level strategy by selecting cost leadership over differentiation in practice.
options.D: Vertical scope by internalising an upstream activity previously purchased externally.

2yr-14.stem: Continuing to rely on Qualcomm under licensing is best classified on the make-or-buy continuum as:

options.A: A make choice because licensing implies internal production and ownership control.
options.B: A parent-subsidiary relation because licensing implies ownership and integration.
options.C: A buy choice using contracts/licensing with residual control rights staying external.
options.D: A joint venture because both parties share governance and operating decisions.

2yr-14.stem: A selective hybrid where Apple makes modems for some SKUs but buys for others is closest to:

options.A: A hybrid governance arrangement that mixes make and buy to preserve benchmarking.
options.B: A full integration choice because any internal production ends external dependence.
options.C: An unrelated diversification choice because the supplier market is separate.
options.D: A pure outsourcing choice because any external sourcing dominates governance form.

2yr-14.stem: Which statement most precisely separates corporate strategy from business strategy in this case?

options.A: Corporate strategy sets HR policy; business strategy sets geography and vertical scope.
options.B: Corporate strategy sets marketing spend; business strategy sets diversification typology only.
options.C: Corporate strategy sets firm boundaries; business strategy sets how to compete within an arena.
options.D: Corporate strategy sets pricing tactics; business strategy sets ownership boundaries and scope.

2yr-14.stem: If Apple internalises to reduce renegotiation hazard and dependence, the best theoretical justification is:

options.A: Platform logic under cross-side network effects and multi-homing behavior.
options.B: Industry life-cycle logic under introduction and shakeout stage pressures.
options.C: Blue-ocean logic under value innovation and new-demand creation dynamics.
options.D: Transaction-cost logic under contracting hazards and asset specificity concerns.

2yr-14.stem: A subtle risk of internalising modems even if per-unit cost falls is:

options.A: Elimination of coordination cost because ownership removes complexity entirely.
options.B: Automatic economies of scope because modems create synergy across unrelated units.
options.C: Guaranteed legal immunity because internal ownership reduces compliance exposure.
options.D: Reduced flexibility when technology standards shift faster than internal capability can adapt.

2yr-14.stem: Acquiring a specialist modem team (tuck-in) is best interpreted as:

options.A: A horizontal diversification into unrelated industries with no device linkage at all.
options.B: A geographic expansion into new markets because talent is distributed globally.
options.C: A business-level positioning move that does not change firm boundaries.
options.D: An instrument to move toward make by buying capability and partial control rights.

2yr-14.stem: Which choice is an example of a boundary alternative to full integration emphasized in Chapter 8?

options.A: Geographic expansion into new countries while keeping sourcing unchanged.
options.B: Long-horizon contracts or equity alliances that align incentives without full ownership.
options.C: Spot-market bidding with frequent switching to maximize short-term flexibility.
options.D: Unrelated diversification into finance to hedge volatility in chip supply markets.

2yr-14.stem: If Apple makes modems for one product line mainly to learn while buying for iPhones, the cleanest label is:

options.A: A geographic scope shift because product lines are sold in different regions.
options.B: A staged hybrid that uses internal production for learning and external sourcing for benchmarking.
options.C: A related diversification move because product lines are different industries in effect.
options.D: A full backward integration move that eliminates reliance on external suppliers fully.

2yr-14.stem: The most disciplined Chapter 8 test for the modem decision is whether:

options.A: Total value created exceeds governance, coordination, and capability-build costs.
options.B: Short-run margin rises, because corporate strategy is always a quarterly choice.
options.C: Competitor imitation occurs quickly, because imitation signals strategic correctness.
options.D: Media sentiment improves, because corporate scope is primarily reputational capital.

2yr-14.stem: A board member argues: 'Licensing is effectively ownership.' The most accurate correction is:

options.A: Ownership is identical to licensing, since both transfer control to the buyer.
options.B: Contracts can reduce hazards, but ownership changes residual control rights and incentives.
options.C: Contracts fully replicate ownership, so governance choice is always irrelevant.
options.D: Licensing removes opportunism entirely, while ownership increases opportunism in practice.

2yr-14.stem: If Apple internalises modems mainly to weaken supplier bargaining power, the motive is closest to:

options.A: Reducing risk by diversifying across unrelated industries and financial assets.
options.B: Increasing market power by reducing dependence on an external bottleneck partner.
options.C: Expanding geographic scope by entering new countries with different regulation.
options.D: Building economies of scope by sharing capabilities across unrelated businesses.

2yr-14.stem: Which option is most likely to increase legal exposure rather than reduce it?

options.A: Using long-horizon contracts with explicit audit rights and service levels.
options.B: Owning and operating sensitive design and compliance processes inside the firm.
options.C: Using a joint venture where liabilities are ring-fenced by governance terms.
options.D: Keeping activity external under licensing with supplier bearing some obligations.

2yr-14.stem: Which is NOT one of Chapter 8's three corporate strategy dimensions?

options.A: Vertical integration scope along the value chain stages.
options.B: Innovation cadence and imitation timing across technology life cycles.
options.C: Geographic scope across regions and national markets.
options.D: Horizontal diversification scope beyond one product-market domain.

2yr-14.stem: Which governance form sits closest to 'make' on the continuum?

options.A: Equity alliance with partial ownership but shared control rights.
options.B: Spot purchasing from multiple suppliers with rapid switching ability.
options.C: Full internal performance of the activity within the firm's boundary.
options.D: Long-term contracting with penalties and audit clauses for performance.

2yr-14.stem: Apple internalising a modem subsystem is vertical integration rather than horizontal diversification because:

options.A: It changes who performs a value-chain activity, not which customer markets are served.
options.B: It adds a new revenue stream, so it is diversification by definition.
options.C: It changes pricing strategy, so it is business strategy by default.
options.D: It expands countries served, so it is geographic scope in most cases.

2yr-14.stem: Which statement best captures why 'make' can raise cost even when the supplier is expensive?

options.A: Internal units always face more competition, which forces costs down sharply.
options.B: Internal units can lose market discipline and create higher overhead over time.
options.C: Internal units eliminate fixed costs because capex disappears in practice.
options.D: Internal units guarantee scale economies bigger than the whole industry.

2yr-14.stem: If Apple expects rapid modem standard shifts, the most defensible first move is often:

options.A: Immediate unrelated diversification to hedge the risk through portfolio logic.
options.B: Hybrid governance that preserves flexibility while building internal capability gradually.
options.C: Immediate geographic expansion because standards vary by country always.
options.D: Immediate full integration because volatility makes contracts unenforceable.

2yr-14.stem: Which is the most accurate description of 'vertical market failure' in Chapter 8?

options.A: Markets create scope economies automatically so diversification is unnecessary in practice at scale.
options.B: Markets are global so vertical integration is legally impossible everywhere in practice at scale.
options.C: Markets along the value chain are too risky and alternatives too costly in time or money.
options.D: Markets are perfectly competitive so the firm should always buy the activity in practice.

2yr-14.stem: If Apple uses long-horizon contracts plus partial internal production, the best label is:

options.A: A pure make choice because internal production exists at least somewhere.
options.B: A geographic scope choice because contracts differ across regions in practice.
options.C: A pure buy choice because any contract implies external governance only.
options.D: A portfolio of governance forms chosen to minimise total transaction and coordination costs.

2yr-14.stem: Which is the best 'non-intuitive' warning when executives say 'control is always good'?

options.A: Control always improves margins because internal costs are always lower.
options.B: Control always eliminates risk because ownership removes uncertainty completely.
options.C: Control can be value destroying when added coordination and rigidity exceed benefits.
options.D: Control always reduces scrutiny because regulators prefer integrated firms.

2yr-14.stem: If Apple buys an unrelated insurance business with no competence transfer, that is:

options.A: Backward vertical integration into upstream component production and supply.
options.B: A geographic scope move because insurance is regulated nationally.
options.C: Forward vertical integration into downstream distribution of device products.
options.D: Unrelated diversification beyond a single market without synergy basis.

options.A: Spinouts always destroy value because internal markets are weakened.
options.B: Geographic expansion always creates synergy, so valuations rise mechanically.
options.C: Shared capabilities create economies of scope that exceed added coordination costs.
options.D: Unrelated businesses reduce risk, so valuations always rise above sum-of-parts.

options.A: Option length is controlled, so correctness depends on concept logic not style.
options.B: Option length signals expertise, so longer options are always correct.
options.C: Option length signals difficulty, so shorter options are always correct.
options.D: Option length is irrelevant because all corporate strategy is subjective.

options.C: A full make strategy because any internal delivery ends all outsourcing.

2yr-17.stem: Introducing spending caps is the clearest example of:

options.A: Output controls that specify results while leaving all means fully flexible.
options.B: Cultural control that relies on shared beliefs rather than formal mechanisms.
options.C: Matrix control that relies on dual reporting lines and program authority.
options.D: Input controls that constrain actions ex ante through explicit rules and budgets.

2yr-17.stem: If Netflix ties bonuses to subscriber retention targets while letting teams choose methods, that is closest to:

options.A: Simple-structure control guiding behavior through direct founder supervision.
options.B: Founder imprinting guiding behavior through the founder’s personal lifestyle.
options.C: Output controls guiding behavior through results rather than prescribed processes.
options.D: Input controls guiding behavior through SOPs and procedural compliance checks.

2yr-17.stem: A non-intuitive risk of strong culture is that it can produce:

options.A: Lower inertia because strong culture prevents success lock-in always.
options.B: Groupthink where dissent is suppressed and assumptions go unchallenged over time.
options.C: Perfect adaptation because strong norms always increase diversity of thought.
options.D: Automatic innovation because strong values eliminate need for exploration.

2yr-17.stem: The best the material example of founder imprinting is:

options.A: A founder shaping enduring norms that persist long after departure from leadership.
options.B: A firm adopting cost leadership by outsourcing production to low-cost regions.
options.C: A board selecting an external auditor to monitor financial reporting accuracy.
options.D: A firm entering a foreign market by franchising rather than investing capital.

2yr-17.stem: Netflix’s culture memo is most accurately an artifact that works because it:

options.A: Replaces hierarchy because artifacts automatically decentralize decision authority in practice.
options.B: Eliminates the need for metrics because text alone directs performance outcomes.
options.C: Makes values and norms explicit, influencing selection, socialization, and reward fit.
options.D: Substitutes for structure because no reporting lines are needed in practice.

2yr-17.stem: If Netflix offers severance to encourage non-fit employees to exit early, it most closely mirrors:

options.A: Matrix escalation routines resolving dual reporting conflicts through committees.
options.B: Zappos-style exit incentives reinforcing cultural fit via employee self-selection.
options.C: OKR peer pressure created solely by public stretch goals and dashboards.
options.D: M-form budgeting allocating corporate capital to SBUs with P&L accountability.

2yr-17.stem: The most precise definition of organizational culture in the material is:

options.A: The set of market forces that determine rivalry and profitability in the industry.
options.B: Formal rules and SOPs that specify each action step for predictable outcomes.
options.C: The organizational chart showing reporting lines and spans of control only.
options.D: Collectively shared values and norms that shape members’ interpretations and actions.

2yr-17.stem: A culture change effort is most likely to fail if Netflix changes slogans but does NOT change:

options.A: Geographic scope, because culture cannot change within one national context.
options.B: Industry structure, because culture shifts require changing rivalry and entry barriers.
options.C: Selection, socialization, and reward systems that reinforce daily behavior patterns.
options.D: Cost drivers, because culture depends only on economies of scale and learning.

2yr-17.stem: Which pair best captures the values–norms distinction?

options.A: Values define industry forces; norms define strategic groups and mobility barriers.
options.B: Values define reporting lines; norms define budgets and input controls always.
options.C: Values define what matters; norms define expected behaviors and attitudes daily.
options.D: Values define specialization; norms define centralization and hierarchy levels.

2yr-17.stem: If Netflix uses senior leaders’ behavior to signal ‘cost discipline’ despite autonomy, that is primarily:

options.A: Output control because role modeling directly defines measurable results.
options.B: Cultural leadership through role modeling, reinforcing norms without formal rules.
options.C: Structural redesign because leader behavior changes the organizational chart.
options.D: Input control because role modeling substitutes for budgets and policies.

2yr-17.stem: Removing ambiguous ‘brilliant jerk’ language is most directly aimed at strengthening:

options.A: Norm clarity so behavioral expectations are less contestable across teams.
options.B: Centralization so approvals move upward and autonomy is reduced fully.
options.C: Hierarchy so spans of control expand and managerial layers increase.
options.D: Formalization so SOPs specify every creative decision step precisely.

2yr-17.stem: A spending cap is classified as input control because it is:

options.A: Considered after the activity and only evaluates outcomes against benchmarks.
options.B: Considered before the value-creating activity and constrains choices ex ante.
options.C: An artifact expressing values but leaving all decisions unconstrained.
options.D: A structural device that reallocates reporting relationships among teams.

2yr-17.stem: Output controls are especially effective when:

options.A: Internal factors make the effort–performance link clear enough to set targets fairly.
options.B: Outcomes are impossible to measure, so goals must remain fully subjective always.
options.C: Collaboration across SBUs is required, because output controls always increase it.
options.D: Employees have no autonomy, so output controls specify every action step.

2yr-17.stem: A subtle drawback of output controls at the corporate level is that they can:

options.A: Reduce the need for structure because charts become irrelevant with targets.
options.B: Replace culture because metrics fully dictate what employees should value in practice.
options.C: Discourage collaboration if units optimize local targets at the expense of shared goals.
options.D: Eliminate conflict because targets provide complete alignment across divisions in practice.

2yr-17.stem: If Netflix formalizes approval gates for content spending, it is most directly increasing:

options.A: Organic coordination through mutual adjustment without rules or documents.
options.B: Decentralization through moving decisions closer to frontline creative staff.
options.C: Specialization through narrower jobs that deepen expertise in content creation.
options.D: Formalization through codified procedures that reduce discretion in spending choices.

2yr-17.stem: Which statement is most correct about strong culture and competitive advantage?

options.A: It never supports advantage because culture is soft and cannot shape outcomes in practice.
options.B: It can support advantage when aligned with strategy, but it can also lock in inertia.
options.C: It always supports advantage because strong values guarantee adaptability always in practice at scale.
options.D: It supports advantage only when accompanied by complete SOP formalization in practice at scale.

2yr-17.stem: Netflix increasing salary bands while keeping autonomy is an example of combining:

options.A: Only structure because salary bands change reporting lines and authority.
options.B: Only culture because pay structures never influence behavior significantly in practice.
options.C: Some input controls with cultural autonomy rather than choosing only one lever.
options.D: Only output controls because salary bands are results-based measures always.

2yr-17.stem: A common mistake when diagnosing ‘culture problems’ is to treat them as purely:

options.A: Messaging issues rather than reinforcement through hiring and reward systems.
options.B: Structure issues rather than values and norms shaping everyday behavior.
options.C: Market issues rather than internal coordination and incentive alignment issues.
options.D: Strategy issues rather than implementation architecture and control choices.

2yr-17.stem: If Netflix wants creativity with cost discipline, the most defensible the material approach is to:

options.A: Adopt full organic design so budgets and caps are removed and costs are ignored.
options.B: Adopt full mechanistic design so creativity is replaced by predictable SOP outcomes in practice.
options.C: Shift to M-form so each show is an SBU with its own CEO and P&L authority.
options.D: Mix loose autonomy norms with targeted input controls on high-risk spend categories in practice.

2yr-17.stem: Which option is NOT a control mechanism emphasized in the material?

options.A: Output controls through targets tied to rewards with flexible execution methods.
options.B: Cultural controls through values and norms shaping behavior informally.
options.C: PESTEL controls through political and ecological forces that managers cannot alter.
options.D: Input controls through budgets and SOPs considered before business decisions.

2yr-17.stem: A robust indicator that culture is changing is that new hires begin to:

options.A: Adopt different cost drivers because learning curves improved quickly.
options.B: Display different day-to-day norms because selection and socialization have shifted.
options.C: Report to different bosses because the organizational chart changed immediately.
options.D: Face different competitors because industry rivalry has structurally transformed.

2yr-17.stem: Which statement about artifacts is correct?

options.A: Artifacts are identical to norms because they directly prescribe attitudes daily.
options.B: Artifacts are visible signals of culture but do not guarantee alignment with behavior.
options.C: Artifacts are identical to values because they define what is important always.
options.D: Artifacts are identical to SOPs because they prescribe each action step.

2yr-17.stem: Boeing tightening detailed build procedures to reduce defects is most directly increasing:

options.A: Decentralization via moving decision authority downward to frontline workers.
options.B: Horizontal diversification via entry into new industries to reduce risk.
options.C: Formalization via codified rules and standard operating procedures for predictability.
options.D: Organic coordination via mutual adjustment without rules or documentation.

2yr-17.stem: In organizational design, a mechanistic design is most appropriate when leaders prioritize:

options.A: Dual reporting to resolve trade-offs between functions and divisions quickly.
options.B: Founder-led improvisation with minimal systems and few specialized functions.
options.C: Predictable outcomes through standardized processes and centralized authority.
options.D: Rapid mutual adjustment through low formalization and decentralized decisions.

2yr-17.stem: If an FAA panel reports ‘employees don’t understand safety initiatives’, the most direct the material lever is to redesign:

options.A: Business-level positioning so Boeing becomes a cost leader in airlines.
options.B: Communication channels and artifacts that translate values and rules into daily norms.
options.C: Corporate scope so Boeing exits aerospace and enters unrelated industries.
options.D: Industry structure to reduce rivalry so managers have time for training.

2yr-17.stem: A safety system that defines expected defect rates but lets plants choose methods is closest to:

options.A: Cultural controls emphasizing founder imprinting through personal frugality.
options.B: Output controls emphasizing results rather than prescribed processes for execution.
options.C: Input controls emphasizing prespecified procedures before work begins always.
options.D: Matrix controls emphasizing dual reporting lines for program accountability.

2yr-17.stem: Which statement best captures organizational inertia in Boeing’s context?

options.A: New failures automatically force reinvention because success is no longer relevant.
options.B: Inertia occurs only in startups because founders centralize decisions too much.
options.C: Past success locks in structures and metrics that resist change under new pressures.
options.D: Inertia occurs only in organic firms because hierarchy prevents accountability in practice.

2yr-17.stem: According to Exhibit 11.2, the step immediately before organizational inertia is:

options.A: Open innovation boundary permeability that increases external idea inflows.
options.B: Ambidexterity balancing exploration and exploitation across time horizons in practice.
options.C: External shifts only, because internal shifts do not affect coupled systems.
options.D: Structures, metrics, and systems that accommodate and manage size and complexity.

2yr-17.stem: If Boeing increases layers of approvals for design changes, it is most directly increasing:

options.A: Decentralization and mutual adjustment that can speed response to local issues.
options.B: Organic collaboration by removing authority and letting teams self-organize.
options.C: Hierarchy and centralization that can slow response but tighten accountability.
options.D: Cross-functional teaming by eliminating dual reporting and program leads.

2yr-17.stem: A non-intuitive risk of extreme mechanistic controls is that they can:

options.A: Remove inertia because compliance systems constantly force redesign cycles.
options.B: Guarantee learning because formalization always increases voice and disclosure.
options.C: Eliminate culture risk because procedures fully replace norms and trust.
options.D: Reduce problem reporting if employees fear blame and merely ‘comply’ superficially.

2yr-17.stem: If Boeing wants both rapid escalation and predictable output, the most defensible design is to:

options.A: Adopt pure organic design so procedures are removed and teams improvise freely.
options.B: Combine mechanistic core procedures with escalation channels and culture for voice.
options.C: Adopt pure matrix design so every employee reports to two bosses always.
options.D: Adopt pure M-form design so each plant becomes fully independent and uncoordinated.

2yr-17.stem: Which of the following is NOT one of the four building blocks of structure in the material?

options.A: Diversification through entry into multiple product markets and industries in practice.
options.B: Centralization through concentration of decision authority higher up the hierarchy.
options.C: Formalization through codified rules and SOPs guiding employee behavior in practice.
options.D: Specialization through division of labor across tasks and expert roles in practice.

2yr-17.stem: Boeing’s ‘disconnect’ finding is most directly a culture problem when it reflects:

options.A: A weakness in cost-driver analysis for cost leadership versus differentiation.
options.B: Misaligned values and norms about safety versus production pressure in daily choices.
options.C: A mismatch between international and multidomestic strategies across countries in practice.
options.D: A lack of divisional CEOs with P&L authority under an M-form structure.

2yr-17.stem: If a plant hides defects to meet output targets, the most accurate diagnosis is:

options.A: A matrix structure problem because two bosses encourage hiding information.
options.B: A simple structure problem because founders would otherwise supervise directly.
options.C: Poorly designed output controls that create gaming and suppress truthful reporting.
options.D: Poorly designed input controls because budgets always cause opportunism.

2yr-17.stem: A balanced scorecard is relevant in the material primarily as an example of:

options.A: A culture artifact that substitutes for reward systems and incentives fully.
options.B: A make-or-buy framework that allocates activities between firms and markets.
options.C: A strategic control system that broadens measurement beyond single financial metrics.
options.D: A structural form that replaces functional departments with SBUs entirely.

2yr-17.stem: Which intervention best reduces retaliation fears without changing the org chart immediately?

options.A: Increase specialization so tasks become narrower and harder to understand in practice.
options.B: Increase centralization so fewer people have information about quality issues in practice.
options.C: Reduce formalization so no one can be held accountable for safety outcomes.
options.D: Protect issue surfacing and reward candor as norms, not only as compliance slogans.

2yr-17.stem: If Boeing’s top managers track only short-term financial metrics, the material predicts a higher risk of:

options.A: Lock-in to success measures that accelerate the inertia pathway under shocks.
options.B: Organic coordination because finance metrics reduce procedural formalization in practice.
options.C: Open innovation because short-term metrics increase boundary permeability in practice.
options.D: Ambidexterity because finance metrics balance exploration and exploitation in practice.

2yr-17.stem: Which statement best captures the ‘virtual cycle’ (Option B) for avoiding inertia?

options.A: One-time reorganization that permanently prevents inertia regardless of future shifts.
options.B: Avoiding reorganization because stability always beats adaptation in practice at scale.
options.C: Continual reorganization to fit internal design to shifting external and internal environments.
options.D: Outsourcing redesign to suppliers so the firm never changes its own systems.

2yr-17.stem: If Boeing redefines safety as a core value but continues rewarding on-time delivery only, the likely outcome is:

options.A: Value–reward misalignment that prevents norms from changing despite rhetoric.
options.B: Lower formalization because rewards reduce the need for SOPs entirely.
options.C: Higher organic design because delivery incentives decentralize decisions.
options.D: Automatic culture change because values always override incentives quickly.

2yr-17.stem: A key difference between input and output controls is that input controls:

options.A: Specify results after action while leaving all methods constrained and fixed.
options.B: Rely on founder imprinting rather than codified procedures and budgets.
options.C: Require matrix dual reporting so supervisors enforce compliance jointly.
options.D: Specify methods and rules before action, aiming for predictable conversion processes.

2yr-17.stem: If Boeing creates cross-functional ‘quality swat teams’ reporting to plant and engineering leaders, this is closest to:

options.A: A pure functional device that eliminates cross-functional interaction entirely in practice.
options.B: A pure simple-structure device that concentrates decisions in the founder.
options.C: A matrix-like coordination device that increases integration but adds role conflict.
options.D: A pure M-form device that makes each team an independent P&L SBU.

2yr-17.stem: Which intervention best targets specialization without changing rules or authority levels?

options.A: Write detailed SOPs so actions are standardized across all workers.
options.B: Add approval layers so decisions must be escalated up the hierarchy.
options.C: Move decision rights downward so frontline teams decide independently in practice.
options.D: Reassign tasks so jobs become narrower and expertise deepens within defined roles.

2yr-17.stem: A key non-intuitive cause of quality failures in a tightly coupled system is that:

options.A: Decentralization always reduces errors because frontline workers know best in practice.
options.B: Organic organizations cannot produce high reliability under any conditions in practice.
options.C: Local workarounds become norms even when formal rules appear adequate on paper.
options.D: Formal rules prevent deviations because employees always comply perfectly in practice.

2yr-17.stem: Which statement best fits the the material view of competitive advantage and design?

options.A: Design matters only for cost leadership because differentiation is purely creative.
options.B: Design matters only for startups because large firms cannot change structures.
options.C: Design can enable advantage by translating strategy into action better than rivals.
options.D: Design is cosmetic because only industry forces determine performance outcomes.

2yr-17.stem: The most non-intuitive way output controls can backfire in a safety setting is by:

options.A: Incentivizing metric manipulation that hides defects instead of fixing root causes.
options.B: Replacing SOPs completely so workers never follow standardized methods.
options.C: Reducing accountability because targets always make managers less responsible.
options.D: Eliminating measurement bias because targets ensure perfect truthfulness in practice.

2yr-17.stem: In organizational design, organizational structure explicitly defines all EXCEPT:

options.A: How resources are distributed to orchestrate work efforts of individuals and teams.
options.B: Which PESTEL forces will shape industry profitability over the next decade.
options.C: Formal communication channels and coordination mechanisms across teams and levels.
options.D: How tasks are divided and integrated through reporting relationships and hierarchy.

2yr-17.stem: Which choice is the most accurate ‘culture-first’ move in Boeing’s case?

options.A: Increase centralization so fewer managers can be questioned by employees.
options.B: Eliminate formalization so no one can be blamed for procedural deviations.
options.C: Make safety-reporting norms salient and protect voice through consistent reward signals.
options.D: Reduce specialization so employees rotate constantly and lose domain expertise.

2yr-17.stem: OpenAI releasing open-weight gpt-oss models is most directly an example of:

options.A: Matrix structure because open weights create dual reporting lines automatically.
options.B: M-form structure because open weights require SBUs with P&L responsibility.
options.C: Open innovation with more permeable boundaries and two-way knowledge flows.
options.D: Closed innovation with impenetrable boundaries and purely internal commercialization.

2yr-17.stem: In organizational design, closed innovation is best defined as a model where the firm:

options.A: Uses only cross-functional teams so functions are eliminated entirely.
options.B: Discovers, develops, and commercializes new products internally behind firm boundaries.
options.C: Relies on acquisitions and equity alliances to outsource R&D continuously.
options.D: Co-develops with external communities and spins off ideas bi-directionally often.

2yr-17.stem: Open innovation differs from closed innovation most precisely because open innovation:

options.A: Allows insourcing and spinning off of ideas, benefiting from external and internal flows.
options.B: Requires strict secrecy so knowledge cannot leak to any external actor.
options.C: Eliminates the need for absorptive capacity because ideas arrive fully packaged.
options.D: Works only with M-form structures and cannot be used in functional organizations.

2yr-17.stem: Absorptive capacity in the material is best described as the firm’s ability to:

options.A: Recognize, assimilate, and apply valuable external knowledge to commercial ends.
options.B: Replace culture with controls so learning becomes a purely procedural activity.
options.C: Outsource knowledge processing so internal teams remain unchanged over time.
options.D: Eliminate external knowledge so the firm focuses only on internal R&D work.

2yr-17.stem: A non-intuitive risk of open-weight releases is that they can:

options.A: Make culture irrelevant because open ecosystems replace internal teamwork fully.
options.B: Eliminate safety risk because transparency guarantees responsible use by all actors.
options.C: Remove the need for structure because communities self-govern without conflict.
options.D: Increase governance costs because external contributions must be curated and verified.

2yr-17.stem: If OpenAI creates an ‘ecosystem engineering’ team to integrate external fixes, the strongest rationale is to build:

options.A: Centralization so all decisions move to the CEO and reduce external variance.
options.B: Hierarchy so managerial layers increase and slow down code integration.
options.C: Specialization so employees become generalists and rotate across roles quickly.
options.D: Absorptive capacity so external ideas can be assimilated and applied reliably.

2yr-17.stem: Which governance move best prevents open innovation from becoming ‘anything goes’?

options.A: Tie pay only to download counts so output controls drive maximal adoption quickly.
options.B: Define contribution standards and review gates as input controls for predictable integration.
options.C: Remove all review so the crowd decides quality without any internal oversight.
options.D: Eliminate values statements so norms do not constrain external contributors in practice.

2yr-17.stem: If OpenAI rewards teams for producing model cards and safety evaluations, it is using:

options.A: Output controls by specifying deliverables while leaving methods open to teams.
options.B: Simple-structure controls by shifting all decisions to the founder only.
options.C: Matrix controls by creating dual reporting and two-boss conflicts deliberately.
options.D: Input controls by prescribing each writing step and forbidding discretion.

2yr-17.stem: Open innovation ‘sharing goes both ways’ most directly implies that firms may:

options.A: Avoid all external interactions because boundary permeability increases inertia in practice.
options.B: Spin off internal ideas but never insource because external ideas are unreliable.
options.C: Insource external ideas while also spinning off internal ideas to external ecosystems.
options.D: Insource external ideas but never share internal ideas due to secrecy requirements.

2yr-17.stem: If OpenAI keeps frontier training closed but releases smaller open-weight models, that is closest to:

options.A: An ambidextrous approach balancing control with selective openness for learning in practice.
options.B: A pure closed innovation model where all outputs and ideas remain internal only.
options.C: A structural shift to M-form where each model becomes a separate SBU.
options.D: A pure open innovation model where all frontier work is fully public always.

2yr-17.stem: Shifting more R&D work to external contributions tends to increase the need for:

options.A: Lower formalization because rules undermine openness and must be removed.
options.B: Higher inertia because openness automatically creates resistance to change.
options.C: Clear coordination mechanisms and interfaces between internal and external actors.
options.D: Lower specialization because everyone must become generalists to absorb code.

2yr-17.stem: Which statement best characterizes open innovation and organizational boundaries?

options.A: Open innovation assumes permeable boundaries, while closed innovation assumes firm-impermeable ones.
options.B: Open innovation assumes impermeable boundaries, while closed innovation assumes permeable ones.
options.C: Both assume impermeable boundaries because IP protection requires secrecy.
options.D: Both assume permeable boundaries because markets force spillovers always.

2yr-17.stem: Licensing under Apache 2.0 to encourage ecosystem uptake is best interpreted as:

options.A: A matrix structure device creating dual reporting inside external firms directly.
options.B: A hierarchy device creating managerial authority over external communities.
options.C: A specialization device reallocating internal tasks into narrower job roles.
options.D: A control-and-culture complement shaping norms without owning contributors in practice.

2yr-17.stem: A classic open-innovation failure mode is ‘not invented here’, best addressed by:

options.A: Higher centralization so external ideas are automatically rejected consistently.
options.B: Culture that rewards adoption of external ideas and reduces status-based resistance.
options.C: Higher hierarchy so fewer employees can access external knowledge directly.
options.D: Lower absorptive capacity so external knowledge cannot enter the firm.

2yr-17.stem: Organizing for innovation in the material most directly concerns aligning design to:

options.A: Eliminate hierarchy permanently because innovation requires zero authority.
options.B: Outsource innovation because internal teams cannot adapt over time.
options.C: Eliminate trade-offs by choosing only mechanistic controls for predictability.
options.D: Support exploration and exploitation across time through ambidextrous practices.

2yr-17.stem: Strict review checklists before merging external pull requests are best classified as:

options.A: Cultural controls relying on beliefs rather than any explicit mechanisms.
options.B: Structural controls changing reporting lines and spans of control immediately.
options.C: Output controls specifying only final results while leaving review optional always.
options.D: Input controls defining acceptable behaviors and procedures before integration decisions.

2yr-17.stem: Measuring ‘time to safe merge’ and rewarding improvement is closest to:

options.A: Input controls tied to SOPs specifying each step of reviewing fully.
options.B: Output controls tied to results with discretion in methods used to improve speed.
options.C: M-form budgeting tied to divisional P&L responsibility in SBUs in practice.
options.D: Founder imprinting tied to CEO habits that substitute for routines in practice.

2yr-17.stem: A subtle advantage of open innovation is that it may:

options.A: Replace internal expertise because external work is always complete and ready.
options.B: Increase idea variety entering the firm, improving exploration options and recombination.
options.C: Eliminate coordination costs because communities self-manage without conflict in practice.
options.D: Guarantee secrecy because transparency prevents competitors learning anything in practice.

2yr-17.stem: Which action would most directly increase absorptive capacity?

options.A: Investing in internal expertise and routines that translate external work into deployment.
options.B: Reducing training so external code can be adopted without internal effort.
options.C: Eliminating documentation so knowledge stays tacit and cannot be copied.
options.D: Banning external collaboration so internal teams focus solely on proprietary work.

2yr-17.stem: If open models create internal friction, the most consistent structural adjustment is to:

options.A: Convert into unrelated SBUs with full P&L independence immediately in practice.
options.B: Clarify interfaces and decision rights for boundary work rather than abandoning openness.
options.C: Move to simple structure so one founder approves all contributions alone.
options.D: Remove all controls so external contributors set priorities without governance.

2yr-17.stem: Open innovation is most likely to fail when the firm lacks:

options.A: Centralization because decentralized decisions always reject external work.
options.B: Absorptive capacity to evaluate, assimilate, and apply external ideas consistently.
options.C: Hierarchy because managers slow innovation and should be removed fully.
options.D: Specialization because experts prevent adoption of external knowledge always.

2yr-17.stem: Which statement is most consistent with the material’s view of controls in open innovation?

options.A: Controls should be purely financial because ecosystems respond only to money.
options.B: Controls should be hidden because transparency undermines trust in communities.
options.C: Controls should enable learning while preventing chaos through gates and feedback loops.
options.D: Controls should be removed because any rule destroys open collaboration always.

2yr-17.stem: If open models increase misuse risk, the most appropriate the material lever is to strengthen:

options.A: Porter positioning because safety is driven primarily by rivalry and entry barriers.
options.B: Control systems and culture to align behavior with safety norms at key interfaces.
options.C: Corporate diversification because risk is best solved by unrelated scope in practice.
options.D: Geographic strategy because safety problems are solved by shifting countries in practice.

2yr-17.stem: Which option is NOT a concept emphasized in the material’s organizing-for-innovation section?

options.A: Absorptive capacity enabling the firm to use valuable outside knowledge sources.
options.B: Open versus closed innovation distinguishing permeable from impenetrable boundaries.
options.C: Ambidexterity balancing exploration and exploitation across different time horizons.
options.D: CAGE distance framework distinguishing cultural and administrative distance globally.

2yr-17.stem: A ‘permeable boundary’ in open innovation most directly increases the need for:

options.A: More inertia because permeability locks the firm into a single external pathway always in practice.
options.B: Less communication because permeability eliminates the need to coordinate workflows in practice at scale in practice.
options.C: Less hierarchy because permeability automatically decentralizes all decisions in practice at scale in practice at scale.
options.D: Clear norms and controls for what is shared, how it is evaluated, and how it is integrated.

2yr-18.stem: A team says: “Because the partner is world-class, Apple’s advantage is guaranteed.” Which evaluator response is most correct?

options.A: They provide a complete implementation plan because advantage is self-executing in practice.
options.B: They show strong evidence discipline by grounding claims in partner reputation only.
options.C: They confuse brand association with a causal mechanism for sustained advantage in practice.
options.D: They demonstrate scenario planning because certainty reduces uncertainty over time in practice.

2yr-18.stem: A slide claims privacy is solved because “users are asked before any request is sent.” The best critique is:

options.A: They misuse market sizing, because privacy is unrelated to adoption outcomes.
options.B: They over-emphasize implementation detail, while high-level strategy is enough here in practice.
options.C: They under-emphasize user autonomy, because consent removes governance needs in practice.
options.D: They treat consent as full risk control, ignoring data flows, incentives, and enforcement.

2yr-18.stem: The team uses three anecdotes from social media as the main proof of user adoption. The most accurate evaluation is:

options.A: Evidence is sufficient if the narrative is persuasive, even without measurement.
options.B: Evidence is high-quality because anecdotes capture lived experience better than data.
options.C: Evidence is low-credibility and not triangulated, so inference is weaker than it appears.
options.D: Evidence is strong if quotes are recent, because recency substitutes for rigor.

2yr-18.stem: A team presents a long list of features but no explicit decision criteria for why each matters. The best diagnosis is:

options.A: They lack a market definition, so competitive advantage cannot exist in principle.
options.B: They lack a CEO endorsement, so cultural alignment and buy-in cannot occur.
options.C: They lack an org chart, so execution is impossible regardless of the feature set.
options.D: They lack a clear evaluative framework linking features to value creation or switching costs.

2yr-18.stem: The team defines the problem as “AI is important.” The strongest critique is:
