options.C: Licensing contracts always reduce IP leakage and reputation loss risks from partners
options.D: Franchising contracts always reduce IP leakage and reputation loss risks from partners

2yr-16.explanation: Higher control reduces reliance on external partners for quality and proprietary know-how. Exporting, licensing, and franchising typically increase partner dependence, elevating reputation and IP risks.

2yr-16.stem: Adding local payment integrations and India-specific compliance features mainly uses local responsiveness to reinforce:

options.A: Cost reductions support focus strategy by narrowing markets to one segment
options.B: Local responsiveness supports cost leadership by standardizing features globally even more
options.C: Cost reductions support differentiation by increasing product variety across countries always
options.D: Local responsiveness supports differentiation by tailoring features to local needs more

2yr-16.explanation: Local responsiveness typically increases differentiation by tailoring the offering to local preferences and requirements. Cost reductions, by contrast, often support cost leadership through standardization and scale.

2yr-16.stem: If bureaucratic hurdles and inconsistent enforcement slow equipment movement into India, which CAGE dimension is most directly increasing?

options.A: Cultural distance rises when both countries share the same language
options.B: Geographic distance rises when aircraft fly faster between two cities
options.C: Economic distance rises when wage levels converge across two markets
options.D: Administrative distance rises when regulations, approvals, and enforcement become uncertain

2yr-16.explanation: Administrative and political distance captures differences in rules, institutions, and enforcement. Bureaucratic uncertainty and inconsistent approvals raise this distance and thus the costs and risks of operating.

2yr-16.stem: Shein needing clearance from multiple regulators for a London IPO most directly illustrates which CAGE dimension?

options.A: Cultural distance from fashion tastes between Asia and Europe for listings
options.B: Administrative distance from cross-border securities rules and state approvals for listings
options.C: Geographic distance from shipping routes between Guangzhou and London for listings
options.D: Economic distance from income gaps between UK and China buyers listing

2yr-16.explanation: Capital-market permissions, offshore listing rules, and state approvals are institutional and political barriers—administrative distance. They can shape feasibility even when customers, tastes, and physical shipping are unchanged.

2yr-16.stem: Shein’s reported supplier diversification toward Brazil and Turkey most closely resembles which ‘why go global’ motive from the chapter?

options.A: Eliminate liability of foreignness by staying within one country today
options.B: Access larger consumer market by relocating suppliers, not sales today
options.C: Develop new competencies by entering biotech clusters for research today
options.D: Access low-cost inputs while reducing policy exposure in China today

2yr-16.explanation: Shifting suppliers is primarily about input economics and risk-adjusted cost—access to cost-effective production capacity while hedging policy shocks tied to one geography.

2yr-16.stem: A firm that manufactures in one country and sells directly to another via cross-border shipments (with few foreign assets) is using:

options.A: Exporting: produce in one country, sell in another directly
options.B: Acquisition: purchase foreign factories and brands for local presence
options.C: Franchising: replicate service outlets through local entrepreneurs abroad widely
options.D: Joint venture: share ownership with host partner in-market equally

2yr-16.explanation: Exporting is producing in one country and selling in another. The other options involve deeper local asset commitments and/or shared governance structures.

2yr-16.stem: Public scrutiny of supply-chain practices that could reduce valuation and trigger consumer backlash is most closely linked to which downside of going global?

options.A: Loss of reputation if governance controversies spill into new markets
options.B: Location economies if overseas factories raise costs and reduce flexibility
options.C: Loss of IP if contract makers copy proprietary designs abroad
options.D: Liability of foreignness if tariff costs vanish and trust rises

2yr-16.explanation: Reputational loss is a key disadvantage of global expansion, especially when supply chains cross jurisdictions with different labor, compliance, and transparency norms that attract public and regulatory attention.

2yr-16.stem: If Shein builds and owns EU fulfillment centers to speed delivery and manage returns, that shift is best characterized as:

options.A: Pure exporting with no assets and no local employees
options.B: Franchising model for apparel outlets run by independent operators
options.C: Licensing agreement granting brand rights to local platform sellers
options.D: Greenfield subsidiary building owned logistics and fulfillment assets there

2yr-16.explanation: Owned fulfillment centers are value-chain assets abroad, consistent with FDI through a subsidiary (often greenfield). Licensing/franchising rely more on partners; pure exporting avoids foreign assets.

2yr-16.stem: Policy changes that remove low-value shipping exemptions and tighten customs treatment primarily increase which kind of ‘distance’ in CAGE terms?

options.A: Administrative distance rises when customs rules change for small parcels abruptly
options.B: Economic distance rises when incomes converge across consumer markets abruptly today
options.C: Geographic distance rises when air freight becomes slower, not faster abruptly
options.D: Cultural distance rises when parcel size preferences differ by region abruptly

2yr-16.explanation: Customs and tax treatments are political-institutional rules. Changing them raises administrative distance and can undermine the economics of cross-border direct-to-consumer fulfillment.

2yr-16.stem: Fast-fashion models often require both ultra-low cost and rapid adaptation to local demand signals. In the cost–responsiveness framework, this points most strongly to:

options.A: Multidomestic strategy duplicating full operations in each national market globally
options.B: Global standardization competing solely on lowest unit cost worldwide today
options.C: International strategy exporting unchanged products with minimal local tailoring globally
options.D: Transnational strategy combining scale efficiencies with rapid local adaptation globally

2yr-16.explanation: High pressure for cost reductions plus high pressure for local responsiveness implies a transnational strategy—simultaneously seeking global scale efficiencies and local adaptation.

2yr-16.stem: If Shein licensed its designs and brand to local producers, which risk would typically rise most sharply?

options.A: IP protection improves because licensees have no access to design files
options.B: Brand reputation risk rises if licensees cut corners on quality abroad
options.C: Coordination costs vanish because licensees report directly to headquarters abroad always
options.D: Tariff exposure disappears because licensing is always treated as domestic abroad

2yr-16.explanation: Licensing trades speed and low investment for reduced control. That often increases brand and quality variance, which heightens reputational risk—especially in consumer-facing categories.

2yr-16.stem: For cross-border platforms, EU data-privacy and consumer-protection enforcement differences most directly map to which CAGE dimension?

options.A: Cultural distance from different fashion colours and seasonal rituals alone
options.B: Administrative distance from data-privacy rules and consumer-protection enforcement shifts quickly
options.C: Geographic distance from longer ocean routes between ports shifts quickly
options.D: Economic distance from GDP gaps between rich and poor markets

2yr-16.explanation: Regulatory requirements and enforcement institutions are administrative/political distance, and they can drive major compliance cost and risk differences across otherwise similar markets.

2yr-16.stem: In the chapter’s semi-globalization indicators, what share of the world’s population are first-generation immigrants?

options.A: Twenty-five percent of people are first-generation immigrants worldwide
options.B: Nine percent of people are first-generation immigrants worldwide
options.C: Three percent of people are first-generation immigrants worldwide
options.D: Fifteen percent of people are first-generation immigrants worldwide

2yr-16.explanation: The chapter uses several low cross-border shares to argue the world is only semi-globalized; one of them is that only about 3% of the world’s population are first-generation immigrants.

2yr-16.stem: Shipping delays and return frictions that materially affect economics most directly contradict which assumption discussed in the chapter?

options.A: Globalization hypothesis that tastes converge across countries much for firms today
options.B: Porter diamond where domestic rivalry raises firm competitiveness strongly over time
options.C: Liability of foreignness that entrants face extra coordination costs over distance
options.D: Death-of-distance hypothesis that geography no longer affects competitiveness much for firms

2yr-16.explanation: The death-of-distance hypothesis suggests geography should not matter much for advantage. Persistent logistics frictions (time, cost, reliability) show geography remains consequential.

2yr-16.stem: If Shein acquired a European retailer for quick legitimacy and distribution, which trade-off is most accurate per the entry-mode continuum?

options.A: Lower control and speed, but higher capital and integration risk for that deal
options.B: Higher control and speed, but lower capital and minimal integration risk for deal
options.C: Higher control and speed, but higher capital and integration risk for that deal
options.D: Lower control and speed, but lower capital and minimal integration risk for deal

2yr-16.explanation: Acquisitions are high-control, high-investment moves that can provide speed (assets, channels) but create integration challenges and require substantial capital commitments.

2yr-16.stem: Adding a Europe-based design hub that feeds trend insights into a global platform is best described as:

options.A: One-way innovation shipping HQ designs abroad with no feedback loops
options.B: Multidomestic strategy by letting each country develop separate brands alone
options.C: Global standardization by eliminating any local input into product design
options.D: Polycentric innovation by adding regional design hubs feeding global platform

2yr-16.explanation: Polycentric innovation draws from multiple hubs. The distinguishing feature is meaningful two-way or multi-way learning rather than HQ-only innovation flows.

2yr-16.stem: The additional compliance overhead and coordination costs Shein faces when operating under unfamiliar EU rules are best captured by:

options.A: Experience curve from output doubling to reduce unit costs
options.B: Liability of foreignness from compliance and coordination in settings
options.C: Economies of scale from serving markets with same platform
options.D: Location economies from locating activity in the best geography

2yr-16.explanation: Liability of foreignness refers to extra costs of operating in unfamiliar environments and coordinating across distance. Compliance regimes and coordination complexity are classic sources of this liability.

2yr-16.stem: If Shein shifts from pure cross-border shipping to owned EU warehouses, which change is most consistent with moving rightward on the investment/control continuum?

options.A: Less control over delivery and returns, but less fixed-cost commitment in each region
options.B: More control over delivery and returns, but less fixed-cost commitment in each region
options.C: More control over delivery and returns, but more fixed-cost commitment in each region
options.D: Less control over delivery and returns, but more fixed-cost commitment in each region

2yr-16.explanation: Owned assets typically increase control over service quality and operational execution, but they also add fixed costs and capital commitment—making exit harder if the strategy fails.

2yr-16.stem: For a fast-fashion ecosystem, world-class logistics providers, textile clusters, and digital marketing complementors most directly map to which element of Porter’s diamond?

options.A: Related industries: strong logistics, textiles, and digital marketing complementors locally
options.B: Factor conditions: abundant oil reserves enabling cheaper clothes production locally
options.C: Demand conditions: sophisticated home buyers demanding avant‑garde couture locally today
options.D: Competitive intensity: one protected champion with no local rivalry pressure

2yr-16.explanation: Related and supporting industries (including complementors) strengthen national competitive advantage by providing inputs, know-how, and ecosystem capabilities that support the focal industry.

2yr-16.stem: A market looks attractive by income, but CAGE indicates very high distance costs. What is the most defensible implication?

options.A: Prefer closer CAGE markets when distance costs overwhelm market-size attractiveness in early entry
options.B: Choose by GDP alone because cultural frictions can be standardized away quickly everywhere
options.C: Ignore CAGE because high-income markets always guarantee high sales in early entry stages
options.D: Prefer farthest markets to maximize learning even if costs spike in early entry

2yr-16.explanation: CAGE highlights that distance creates costs/risks that can dominate otherwise attractive markets. A nearer market can yield better realized performance even if its absolute GDP is lower.

2yr-16.stem: Which option is the best definition of ‘global strategy’ as used in the chapter?

options.A: Business-level choice to price below rivals in one local market only
options.B: Operational choice to schedule shifts on a single factory line only
options.C: Corporate-level choices to compete and win against firms worldwide over time
options.D: Functional choice to design advertising slogans for one country audience only

2yr-16.explanation: Global strategy is part of corporate strategy aimed at gaining and sustaining advantage while competing globally—across foreign and domestic rivals and multiple countries.

2yr-16.stem: Which option best matches the chapter’s definition of a multinational enterprise (MNE)?

options.A: MNE: holds foreign stocks but does not manage any subsidiaries abroad
options.B: MNE: sells only domestically but imports some inputs occasionally for production
options.C: MNE: deploys resources to procure, produce, and distribute in ≥2 countries
options.D: MNE: earns revenue abroad but has no operations outside home base

2yr-16.explanation: An MNE deploys resources/capabilities in procurement, production, and/or distribution in at least two countries. Mere foreign revenue or portfolio holdings are not sufficient by themselves.

2yr-16.stem: Which option best captures ‘globalization’ as defined in the chapter?

options.A: Complete disappearance of borders making firms identical across all markets everywhere today
options.B: Only rising tariffs and higher shipping costs reducing all trade volumes now
options.C: Closer cross-country integration enabled by lower barriers and cheaper coordination technology overall
options.D: Purely cultural convergence where languages merge into one global dialect over time

2yr-16.explanation: Globalization is closer integration and exchange among countries, enabled by falling barriers and advances in telecommunications and transportation. It does not imply borders vanish entirely.

2yr-16.stem: When counterfeit versions of designs proliferate in a foreign market, which disadvantage of going global is most directly highlighted?

options.A: Reputation risk rises when sales growth causes overcapacity in factories
options.B: Location economies vanish when firms move production nearer to customers
options.C: Liability costs fall when firms enter culturally distant markets quickly
options.D: IP loss rises when designs get copied and scaled locally

2yr-16.explanation: The chapter highlights loss of intellectual property as a downside of operating internationally, especially when local actors can copy, reverse-engineer, or counterfeit products and designs.

2yr-16.stem: Which statement correctly distinguishes a joint venture from an equity alliance in the chapter’s entry-mode menu?

options.A: Equity alliance forms a new entity with shared ownership and governance rules
options.B: Joint venture forms a new entity with shared ownership and governance rules
options.C: Licensing forms a new entity with shared ownership and governance rules today
options.D: Exporting forms a new entity with shared ownership and governance rules today

2yr-16.explanation: A joint venture typically creates a separate entity with shared ownership and governance. An equity alliance involves ownership stakes without necessarily forming a new jointly owned operating entity.

2yr-16.stem: If Shein buys a 20% stake in a European logistics start-up to secure capacity, what entry arrangement is most accurately described?

options.A: Joint venture using fifty-fifty ownership to create new company
options.B: Licensing contract giving logistics partner rights to Shein brand
options.C: Equity alliance using minority ownership to secure strategic access
options.D: Exporting arrangement shipping garments through independent carriers only there

2yr-16.explanation: A minority equity stake to secure strategic access is an equity alliance. A joint venture implies shared control and often a new entity; licensing and exporting are non-equity arrangements.

2yr-16.stem: Localizing size charts, payment methods, and return policies primarily addresses which pressure in the cost–responsiveness framework?

options.A: Factor-conditions effect from natural resources that support lower material cost abroad
options.B: Demand-conditions effect from sophisticated domestic customers in the home market alone
options.C: Local responsiveness pressure from different sizing norms and return expectations abroad
options.D: Cost-reduction pressure from duplicating warehouses and teams in every country abroad

2yr-16.explanation: These actions tailor the offering and customer experience to local preferences and requirements, indicating pressure for local responsiveness (often supporting differentiation).

2yr-16.stem: In the chapter’s semi-globalization evidence, what share of voice-calling minutes are cross-border?

options.A: Only three percent of voice-calling minutes are cross-border globally today
options.B: Only nine percent of voice-calling minutes are cross-border globally today
options.C: Only eighteen percent of voice-calling minutes are cross-border globally today
options.D: Only two percent of voice-calling minutes are cross-border globally today

2yr-16.explanation: The chapter uses very low cross-border calling shares (about 2%) as one indicator that the world is not ‘fully flat’ but semi-globalized.

2yr-16.stem: U.S. export controls that force Nvidia to redesign China-facing chips primarily increase which pressure in the cost–responsiveness framework?

options.A: Pressure for local responsiveness due to host-country requirements and constraints rising
options.B: Pressure for local responsiveness due to converging global consumer tastes alone
options.C: Pressure for cost reductions due to higher wages in home country
options.D: Pressure for cost reductions due to scale economies in one design

2yr-16.explanation: In the chapter, local responsiveness includes tailoring to host-country requirements—not only consumer tastes. Export controls are regulatory requirements that force product tailoring by market, raising local-responsiveness pressure.

2yr-16.stem: Export controls and licensing constraints are a clear example of which CAGE distance being ‘weaponised’?

options.A: Cultural distance shaped by language barriers between engineers alone
options.B: Economic distance shaped by income gaps between data-center buyers
options.C: Administrative distance shaped by security-driven trade and export rules
options.D: Geographic distance shaped by longer flights between chip fabs

2yr-16.explanation: Export rules are political-institutional barriers. They increase administrative distance by constraining what can be sold, to whom, and under what monitoring and enforcement regime.

2yr-16.stem: For Nvidia, export controls most directly reduce which textbook advantage of competing internationally?

options.A: Access to low-cost inputs becomes impossible because chips are heavy today
options.B: Access to larger markets becomes constrained by export licensing caps today
options.C: Developing new competencies becomes impossible because engineers cannot travel freely today
options.D: Location economies vanish because every country has identical capabilities now already

2yr-16.explanation: Export controls restrict market access regardless of customer demand, directly undermining the ‘larger market’ advantage. Input-factor access and competence building can still occur, though with added friction.

2yr-16.stem: If hardware exports are constrained, a firm might consider technology licensing to local partners. Which trade-off is most accurate?

options.A: Higher capital, slower access, but higher IP leakage and control loss overall risk
options.B: Lower capital, faster access, but lower IP risk and higher control overall risk
options.C: Lower capital, faster access, but higher IP leakage and control loss overall risk
options.D: Higher capital, slower access, but lower IP risk and higher control overall risk

2yr-16.explanation: Licensing is low-investment and can speed presence, but it reduces control and can increase IP leakage risk. Higher-control modes protect IP better but require more capital and may be blocked by policy.

2yr-16.stem: The chapter’s note that cutting-edge chip supply is concentrated in one geography implies what strategic risk for MNEs?

options.A: Supply concentration raises geopolitical risk; disruption can halt global electronics quickly today
options.B: Supply concentration eliminates risk because one supplier guarantees uniform standards always everywhere
options.C: Supply concentration lowers costs but also removes any need for inventory buffers
options.D: Supply concentration mainly increases cultural distance between buyers and engineers in chips

2yr-16.explanation: When critical supply is geographically concentrated, firms face geopolitical and operational disruption risk (e.g., conflict, sanctions, logistics shocks). This is a global-strategy vulnerability beyond simple cost calculus.

2yr-16.stem: A dense cluster of specialized semiconductor suppliers, tooling, and advanced packaging expertise best maps to which element of Porter’s diamond?

options.A: Competitive intensity absent, with one protected firm and no rivals there
options.B: Related industries with dense supplier clusters, tooling, and packaging expertise nearby
options.C: Demand conditions from domestic Taiwan consumers buying many high-end chips alone
options.D: Factor conditions from large oil reserves financing chip fabrication plants there

2yr-16.explanation: Related and supporting industries (and complementors) strengthen national competitive advantage by providing ecosystem capabilities. Semiconductor competitiveness often depends on clusters of suppliers and specialized services.

2yr-16.stem: Centralizing R&D and production for scale, while offering only compliance-driven variants by market, is closest to which global strategy?

options.A: Global standardization emphasizing scale, centralized R&D, and minimal localization overall today
options.B: International strategy emphasizing exports from home and low cost pressure only
options.C: Transnational strategy emphasizing deep localization plus global integration simultaneously overall today
options.D: Multidomestic strategy emphasizing independent country labs and production footprints overall today

2yr-16.explanation: Global standardization focuses on scale and centralized activities to reduce cost. Small compliance variants do not necessarily imply a transnational approach unless local adaptation is deep and systematic.

2yr-16.stem: Which difference from the earlier Cold War is emphasized in the chapter’s ‘techno cold war’ framing?

options.A: Unlike USSR, China is isolated economically and trades little with U.S today overall
options.B: Unlike USSR, China relies only on oil exports and not technology imports today
options.C: Unlike USSR, China depends on U.S. protection alliances to sustain growth today overall
options.D: Unlike USSR, China rivals U.S. GDP and is trade‑interdependent in critical goods today

2yr-16.explanation: The chapter highlights both China’s near-peer economic scale and deep U.S.–China codependence in trade and technology, distinguishing the techno cold war from the USSR-era Cold War.

2yr-16.stem: Under techno cold war conditions, what new screening factor becomes central in ‘where to compete’ decisions?

options.A: Country choice must include political alignment, not only market potential anymore today
options.B: Country choice should be random because distance never influences global outcomes today
options.C: Country choice should focus solely on geographic proximity to headquarters today only
options.D: Country choice can ignore politics because trade rules are stable worldwide today

2yr-16.explanation: When export controls and security logics spread across blocs, political alignment and policy predictability become decisive constraints alongside economic attractiveness and CAGE distances.

2yr-16.stem: Which entry mode gives the highest design/control over facilities and culture, but often the slowest ramp-up?

options.A: Licensing: highest control over design, but slowest build-out often in practice today
options.B: Greenfield subsidiary: highest control over design, but slowest build-out often in practice
options.C: Exporting: highest control over design, but slowest build-out often in practice today
options.D: Franchising: highest control over design, but slowest build-out often in practice today

2yr-16.explanation: Greenfield subsidiaries require building from scratch, which is slower but allows the firm to design operations and culture. Exporting/licensing/franchising are lower-investment and do not provide the same facility control.

2yr-16.stem: Pursuing country-specific chip variants to satisfy local rules can undermine which benefit associated with cost reductions?

options.A: It can remove cultural distance, aligning buyer preferences across markets overall
options.B: It can eliminate regulatory risk, making tariffs irrelevant to strategy overall
options.C: It can create location economies by centralizing everything in one country
options.D: It can erode scale economies, raising unit costs of production overall

2yr-16.explanation: High local responsiveness often increases costs by fragmenting volumes and duplicating efforts, which can erode scale economies. This is one reason balancing both pressures is difficult.

2yr-16.stem: Monitoring and inspection requirements attached to exports primarily add what, according to the chapter’s concept set?

options.A: Higher demand conditions in home market, improving national competitive advantage for chips
options.B: Added compliance and coordination costs, strengthening liability of foreignness abroad for exporters
options.C: Lower factor conditions, reducing infrastructure and human capital in host for chips
options.D: Reduced compliance costs, weakening liability of foreignness abroad for exporters over time

2yr-16.explanation: Compliance-heavy exporting and cross-border coordination increase the costs of operating across jurisdictions, consistent with liability of foreignness (unfamiliar institutions and coordination across distance).

2yr-16.stem: In the chapter’s semi-globalization indicators, what share of internet traffic crosses national borders?

options.A: Seventy percent of internet traffic crosses national borders worldwide today
options.B: Thirty percent of internet traffic crosses national borders worldwide today
options.C: Fifty percent of internet traffic crosses national borders worldwide today
options.D: Eighteen percent of internet traffic crosses national borders worldwide today

2yr-16.explanation: The chapter cites that only about 18% of internet traffic is cross-border, reinforcing the argument that the world remains semi-globalized rather than fully ‘flat.’

2yr-16.stem: If the world bifurcates into rival technology blocs, what global-strategy implication is most defensible for MNEs?

options.A: Prepare only marketing adaptation because hardware trade barriers will disappear over time
options.B: Prepare single global supply chain because blocs always reconverge quickly over time
options.C: Prepare to exit all foreign markets because semi-globalization forbids trade over time
options.D: Prepare dual supply chains and standards for separate geopolitical blocs over time

2yr-16.explanation: Strategic bifurcation can force firms to operate parallel supply chains, standards, and compliance regimes. Single-stack assumptions become fragile when policy and standards diverge by bloc.

2yr-16.stem: Locating an AI research lab in a top talent cluster to learn faster is best explained by which concept?

options.A: Location economies from placing R&D where talent clusters concentrate
options.B: Economies of scale from serving markets with same platform
options.C: Globalization hypothesis from converging tastes for AI chips globally
options.D: Liability of foreignness from operating only in domestic markets

2yr-16.explanation: Location economies refer to benefits from locating a specific value-chain activity in the geography that offers the best conditions for that activity—here, talent and knowledge spillovers.

2yr-16.stem: Which motive for going global is most directly served when an MNE relocates R&D to join a learning cluster?

options.A: Develop new competencies by embedding in global learning communities for advantage
options.B: Access larger markets by reducing administrative distance via tariffs for advantage
options.C: Access low-cost inputs by relocating production to higher-wage areas for advantage
options.D: Avoid all foreign risks by keeping operations strictly domestic for advantage

2yr-16.explanation: The chapter notes that firms often expand internationally to develop new competencies by joining communities of learning in specific regions (clusters), especially for differentiation-driven advantages.

2yr-16.stem: Which condition most strongly supports a global-standardization approach for a technology product?

options.A: When costs are irrelevant because buyers pay any price for chips globally
options.B: When suppliers are local monopolies and firms can ignore rivals easily globally
options.C: When customer needs are similar and scale economies are large globally today
options.D: When customer needs differ strongly and governments mandate local adaptation globally today

2yr-16.explanation: Global standardization fits when customer needs are relatively homogeneous and scale economies are large, making centralized, standardized offerings cost-effective.

2yr-16.stem: When export controls make one market risky, the most defensible reallocation principle is to:

options.A: Reallocate output to markets with equal distance, since distance never matters
options.B: Reallocate scarce output to markets with higher administrative distance and uncertainty
options.C: Reallocate scarce output to markets with lower administrative distance and certainty
options.D: Reallocate scarce output to markets with lowest geographic distance only always

2yr-16.explanation: Administrative distance and policy predictability can dominate other attractiveness metrics under export controls. Firms tend to prioritize markets where rules are clearer and enforcement risk lower.

2yr-16.stem: Which statement best reflects the chapter’s claim about national competitive advantage?

options.A: World-leading home industries imply geography never matters for competitive advantage again today
options.B: World-leading home industries guarantee firms face no liability of foreignness abroad ever
options.C: World-leading home industries prevent firms from expanding because markets saturate quickly abroad
options.D: World-leading home industries produce firms that compete strongest internationally over many years

2yr-16.explanation: National competitive advantage—world leadership in specific industries—tends to produce globally strong competitors. It does not eliminate foreignness liabilities, nor does it make geography irrelevant.

2yr-16.stem: Within Porter’s diamond, what is the most direct mechanism by which intense domestic rivalry helps global competitiveness?

options.A: Domestic rivalry reduces innovation because firms collude and avoid competition there
options.B: Domestic rivalry matters only when natural resources are abundant there always
options.C: Domestic rivalry pushes rapid innovation, strengthening global competitiveness of firms there
options.D: Domestic rivalry matters only when customers abroad are sophisticated buyers there

2yr-16.explanation: Competitive intensity at home pressures firms to improve, innovate, and contain costs—capabilities that can translate into stronger performance in global markets.

2yr-16.stem: The chapter highlights U.S.–China ‘codependence’ in trade and technology. Which pairing best matches that claim?

options.A: U.S. depends on China for aircraft engines; China depends on West for snow sports
options.B: U.S. depends on China for oil exports; China depends on U.S. for rice imports
options.C: U.S. depends on China for manufactured goods; China depends on West for chips designs
options.D: U.S. depends on China for language services; China depends on West for tourism only

2yr-16.explanation: The chapter’s argument is that interdependence remains deep: the U.S. relies on Chinese manufacturing, while China still depends on advanced Western technologies such as cutting-edge chip design and equipment.

2yr-16.stem: In the chapter’s CAGE discussion, how does geographic distance affect trade volume in the cited comparison?

options.A: Countries 5,000 miles apart trade only with identical languages and cultures today always
options.B: Countries 5,000 miles apart trade the same as any distance at all today
options.C: Countries 5,000 miles apart trade about one‑fifth as much as 1,000 mile pairs
options.D: Countries 5,000 miles apart trade about twice as much as nearby pairs today

2yr-16.explanation: The chapter uses distance elasticities to show that geography still matters: longer distances sharply reduce trade volumes, even before adding cultural and administrative distances.

2yr-16.stem: Rising wages in an offshoring destination can have what effect on the original ‘low-cost input factor’ advantage?

options.A: Rising wages make administrative distance disappear, removing tariffs worldwide at once today
options.B: Rising wages can expand low-cost advantages, making offshoring more attractive to China
options.C: Rising wages can erode low-cost advantages that first motivated offshoring to China
options.D: Rising wages remove cultural distance, aligning preferences across all nations today fully

2yr-16.explanation: As wages rise, the cost advantage that motivated offshoring can shrink or disappear, prompting firms to re-optimise location choices or invest in automation and productivity.

2yr-16.stem: The chapter notes that only a small share of an iPhone’s value is added in final assembly. What is that approximate share?

options.A: About thirty percent of iPhone value is added in assembly
options.B: About fifteen percent of iPhone value is added in assembly
options.C: About five percent of iPhone value is added in assembly
options.D: About fifty percent of iPhone value is added in assembly

2yr-16.explanation: The chapter uses the iPhone example to show how little value can be captured by low-margin assembly relative to upstream design and key components, reinforcing the ‘Designed vs Made’ distinction.

2yr-16.stem: When an international partner uses transferred know-how to create competing products and undercut the original firm, which downside of going global is most directly illustrated?

options.A: Loss of reputation when partners mistreat workers and damage brand after transfer
options.B: Location economies when firms relocate activity to optimal geographies worldwide for savings
options.C: Loss of intellectual property when partners learn and compete globally after transfer
options.D: Liability of foreignness when firms avoid foreign markets and stay home always

2yr-16.explanation: The chapter’s IP-loss examples show how partners can ‘learn’ and then compete. This is distinct from reputational loss and from the generic foreignness costs of operating abroad.

2yr-20.stem: In Caselet A, which statement most precisely frames the core principal–agent tension?

options.A: Investors delegate scientific oversight to regulators who may privilege disclosure over safety duties.
options.B: Executives delegate legal ownership to employees who may privilege mission over revenue targets.
options.C: A nonprofit board delegates operating control to executives who may privilege scale over mission.
options.D: Customers delegate model auditing to vendors who may privilege speed over evaluative accuracy.

2yr-20.stem: Which condition in Caselet A most amplifies the risk of managerial opportunism in agency theory terms?

options.A: Activist investors can buy shares cheaply after price drops and threaten takeover discipline quickly.
options.B: Analysts and auditors can scrutinize SEC filings and reduce misreporting through disclosure pressure.
options.C: Shareholders differ in horizons, causing heterogeneous goals that boards must aggregate imperfectly.
options.D: Managers hold time-sensitive private partnership information before boards and outsiders can verify it.

2yr-20.stem: Which post-crisis change is best classified as an internal corporate governance mechanism (not an external one)?

options.A: Mandating an independent compliance monitor appointed through a government settlement process.
options.B: Reconstituting the board’s membership and chair role to improve monitoring of top management.
options.C: Using public analysts’ consensus forecasts to discipline management through valuation sensitivity.
options.D: Threatening a hostile takeover by stock accumulation to replace management and restructure assets.

2yr-20.stem: Microsoft’s nonvoting observer seat on the board is best interpreted as which governance move?

options.A: A poison-pill provision that automatically dilutes a hostile acquirer once ownership crosses a threshold.
options.B: A leveraged-buyout mechanism that shifts ownership from dispersed shareholders to a private sponsor.
options.C: A GAAP-based disclosure requirement that standardizes reporting and reduces accounting discretion.
options.D: A hybrid monitoring device that increases oversight without transferring formal board voting authority.

2yr-20.stem: Suppose executives’ bonuses are tied only to short-term user growth. Which risk is most consistent with the CEO-pay discussion?

options.A: Incentives eliminate moral hazard because agents internalize all costs of risky strategic decisions.
options.B: Incentives prevent information asymmetry because principals can observe effort through outcomes.
options.C: Incentives can reinforce short-termism at the expense of long-term viability and ethical risk control.
options.D: Incentives resolve adverse selection because candidates self-sort perfectly into high-fit roles.

2yr-20.stem: A candidate oversells expertise in AI safety tooling during recruitment and is hired. Which agency problem is most directly illustrated?

options.A: Thin markets: too few buyers and sellers exist to match supply and demand in time and space.
options.B: Winner’s curse: the firm overpays in a takeover because it misestimates post-deal synergies.
options.C: Adverse selection: information asymmetry raises the chance of selecting an inferior alternative.
options.D: Moral hazard: the hired agent can do the work but chooses to shirk effort once employed.

2yr-20.stem: A research scientist uses company compute for a personal side venture while meeting minimal assigned outputs. Which pairing is best?

options.A: Adverse selection plus stricter background checks, because the true capability was hidden before contracting.
options.B: Thin markets plus better search, because the scientist cannot find collaborators without a platform.
options.C: Moral hazard plus stronger monitoring of effort and resource use, because actions are hidden after contracting.
options.D: Winner’s curse plus takeover defenses, because the firm is at risk of being acquired at a premium.

2yr-20.stem: Which concern is most specific to CEO-chairperson duality as discussed in the governance section?

options.A: The chair must be an outside director, which eliminates internal information flows to the board.
options.B: The chair’s role is primarily to file SEC documents, creating disclosure overload and slow decisions.
options.C: The chair can shape agendas and director selection, weakening the board’s ability to evaluate the CEO.
options.D: The chair’s role is to negotiate supplier contracts, creating operational micromanagement by directors.

2yr-20.stem: A manager argues: “If data collection is legal, it is ethical.” Which reply best reflects the ethics discussion?

options.A: Legality is irrelevant; any profitable tactic is ethical if it increases shareholder returns quickly.
options.B: Legality is a minimum; actions can be lawful yet ethically questionable under societal norms.
options.C: Legality is identical to fairness; therefore legal compliance guarantees reciprocity and honesty.
options.D: Legality is sufficient; ethics is only a personal preference and not a business-relevant standard.

2yr-20.stem: In a high-pressure product culture, leaders quietly reward those who bypass safety reviews. Which diagnosis best fits the chapter’s logic?

options.A: A long tail: many small ethical violations accumulate, so the system becomes profitable but less popular.
options.B: A thin market: safety reviewers and product teams cannot find each other, so corners are cut structurally.
options.C: A bad barrel: organizational context and leadership cues normalize unethical choices beyond a few individuals.
options.D: A bad apple: a few rogue engineers are sufficient explanation if the mission statement mentions integrity.

2yr-20.stem: Which board and leadership action most directly supports an ethical climate consistent with the chapter’s recommendations?

options.A: Outsource ethics to external auditors and remove internal codes to avoid conflicting standards.
options.B: Publish a values poster while keeping performance targets unrealistic to maintain competitive pressure.
options.C: Focus only on legal compliance and avoid discussing broader norms to reduce employee ambiguity.
options.D: Align formal values with informal rewards and set achievable goals that can be met with legal means.

2yr-20.stem: In the business-model framework, which prompt corresponds most directly to revenue and cost logic?

options.A: What activities must be performed to create and deliver offerings to customers reliably?
options.B: How are activities linked and sequenced so the offering is created and delivered consistently?
options.C: Who are the key stakeholders performing the activities that deliver the offerings end to end?
options.D: Why does the model create value, in terms of revenue streams and cost structure?

2yr-20.stem: In the same framework, which prompt targets the concrete work that must happen to deliver the offering?

options.A: What activities need to be performed to create and deliver the offering to customers?
options.B: Who are the stakeholders that execute and govern the activities across the value system?
options.C: Why does the business model create value, considering its revenue and cost architecture?
options.D: How are the activities linked so that delivery quality remains consistent at scale?

2yr-20.stem: In the business-model framework, which prompt is most about assigning roles across partners, suppliers, and internal teams?

options.A: How are activities linked to create the offering across time, geography, and interfaces?
options.B: Who are the main stakeholders performing the activities that enable the offering?
options.C: Why does the offering create value, given pricing, volume, and unit economics constraints?
options.D: What activities are required to produce the offering and ensure customer experience quality?

2yr-20.stem: In the business-model framework, which prompt is most about the architecture that connects activities into a system?

options.A: How are the offerings created by linking activities across teams, partners, and technologies?
options.B: Why does the model create value through its combined revenue design and cost structure choices?
options.C: What activities must be performed to create and deliver the offering with reliable service levels?
options.D: Who are the core stakeholders performing activities, from suppliers through customers and partners?

2yr-20.stem: Which statement best distinguishes strategy from a business model as used in the chapter?

options.A: Strategy is the org chart; the business model is the board structure and SEC reporting cadence.
options.B: Strategy sets goal-directed choices; the business model translates those choices into actionable tactics to make money.
options.C: Strategy is a cost model; the business model is a takeover defense that deters hostile bidders.
options.D: Strategy is the pricing plan; the business model is the mission statement and value poster for employees.

2yr-20.stem: A product offers a basic tier free and charges for advanced features and support. Which business model is the closest match?

options.A: Subscription, because all users pay regardless of usage during the access period by default.
options.B: Agency, because a retailer sells at a commission while the producer controls price strictly.
options.C: Freemium, because a zero-price base expands adoption while premium features monetize power users.
options.D: Wholesale, because retailers set their own prices and profit from the publisher’s fixed discount.

2yr-20.stem: Users pay only for compute consumed, billed per unit of usage. Which business model is the best fit?

options.A: Pay-as-you-go, because charges scale with actual consumption rather than fixed access terms.
options.B: Ultra-low cost, because the firm minimizes service and sells upgrades at premium add-ons.
options.C: Bundling, because negatively correlated demands are combined and sold at a discount price.
options.D: Subscription, because users buy access for a period regardless of whether they consume much.

2yr-20.stem: A company sells a device near cost but earns margins on proprietary replacement consumables. Which model is most accurate?

options.A: Bundling, because multiple products with negatively correlated demand are sold together at discount.
options.B: Razor–razor blades, because the initial product stimulates demand for profitable complementary replacements.
options.C: Agency, because an intermediary sells on commission while the producer sets a controlled retail price.
options.D: Wholesale, because the producer sells to retailers at a fixed discount from recommended price.

2yr-20.stem: Which governance lever most directly represents the external ‘market for corporate control’ as described?

options.A: Inside directors provide operational information and help the board understand internal performance limits.
options.B: Boards approve budgets and oversee stakeholder relations while CEOs manage day-to-day operations.
options.C: Stock options align incentives by letting executives buy shares at a predetermined strike price later.
options.D: Activist investors accumulate shares to gain control and replace management in an underperforming firm.

2yr-20.stem: A listed firm adopts a provision allowing existing shareholders to buy extra shares cheaply once an acquirer crosses a threshold. What is it?

options.A: A thin-market fix, because search frictions fall when transaction costs approach near zero.
options.B: A subscription model, because access is sold for a time period irrespective of usage volume.
options.C: A poison pill, because dilution makes a hostile takeover materially more expensive for the bidder.
options.D: A leveraged buyout, because debt financing enables taking the firm private through share purchase.

2yr-20.stem: A private-equity sponsor buys all outstanding shares using borrowed money secured by the target’s assets and delists the company. This is:

options.A: A poison pill, because shareholders can buy discounted shares once ownership crosses a threshold.
options.B: An agency model, because a retailer sells at commission while the producer controls retail pricing.
options.C: A long-tail strategy, because niche products with low unit sales accumulate into large revenue.
options.D: A leveraged buyout, because leverage is used to purchase shares and shift ownership from public to private.

2yr-20.stem: Why can industry analyst recommendations be systematically biased, even when they use public filings?

options.A: Bias is eliminated when boards appoint more inside directors who can explain the firm’s internal logic.
options.B: Conflicts of interest vanish because EDGAR filings are standardized under GAAP and publicly searchable.
options.C: Bias is irrelevant because ethical conduct is fully captured by legal compliance in disclosure forms.
options.D: Conflicts of interest can arise because analysts’ firms may have lucrative relationships with rated companies.

2yr-20.stem: A platform sells countless niche digital items; each sells rarely, but collectively they generate substantial revenue. Which concept fits best?

options.A: Short head, because most revenue comes from a few blockbuster hits supported by heavy marketing budgets.
options.B: Long tail, because near-zero marginal cost and good search aggregate many low-volume items into large sales.
options.C: Adverse selection, because agents misrepresent capabilities during recruitment and screening processes.
options.D: Winner’s curse, because paying a premium for an acquisition destroys value after deal completion.

2yr-20.stem: Which platform feature most directly helps overcome ‘thin markets’ as defined in the chapter?

options.A: CEO-chair duality that accelerates board decisions by concentrating authority in one senior leader.
options.B: A poison pill that deters hostile acquirers by making takeover attempts more expensive to execute.
options.C: Digitization plus strong search and inventory tools that match buyers and sellers across time and geography.
options.D: Bundling of negatively correlated products so each customer buys a discounted multi-product suite.

2yr-20.stem: In Caselet B, the contested practice is best categorized as which governance mechanism?

options.A: Executive compensation, because boards design pay packages to align managers with shareholder interests.
options.B: Market for corporate control, because hostile bids discipline managers through takeover threats.
options.C: Financial statement auditing, because GAAP compliance is verified by certified public accountants.
options.D: Long-tail innovation, because niche offerings collectively generate substantial revenue streams.

2yr-20.stem: Which pair matches the two CEO-pay issues singled out in the governance section?

options.A: CEO tenure relative to board tenure, and the percentage of inside directors on compensation committees.
options.B: CEO pay volatility relative to stock volatility, and the use of bundling to sell compensation packages.
options.C: CEO pay secrecy relative to competitors, and the frequency of SEC filings for compensation disclosure.
options.D: Absolute CEO pay relative to average employee pay, and the pay–performance relationship’s strength.

2yr-20.stem: Behavioral evidence cautions that very high-powered incentives can sometimes reduce performance mainly because they:

options.A: Prevent moral hazard by forcing agents to internalize all downside losses of risky projects.
options.B: Eliminate information asymmetry by making effort perfectly observable through measurable outcomes.
options.C: Remove adverse selection by ensuring only the most capable candidates accept performance pay.
options.D: Distract attention toward the outsized near-term bonus and increase stress, reinforcing short-termism.

2yr-20.stem: A board grants stock options with a strike price set at the grant date. Under agency theory, the primary intent is to:

options.A: Eliminate takeover threats because higher pay makes hostile bidders less interested in acquisitions.
options.B: Replace the need for outside directors because managers now have identical preferences to investors.
options.C: Align managers with owners by tying upside to share-price appreciation above a predetermined threshold.
options.D: Guarantee dividends by reallocating profits from reinvestment into fixed quarterly shareholder payouts.

2yr-20.stem: Which statement best captures why CEO-chair duality can weaken governance, even when decision speed improves?

options.A: GAAP standards no longer apply, so auditors cannot compare performance across firms consistently.
options.B: Inside directors become illegal under SEC rules, so the board loses information needed for oversight.
options.C: Agenda control and friendly appointments can reduce the board’s independence in evaluating CEO performance.
options.D: Hostile takeovers become impossible, so the market for corporate control no longer functions at all.

2yr-20.stem: A hedge fund accumulates shares and demands a spin-out to boost near-term valuation. Which shareholder-horizon fact is most relevant?

options.A: Shareholders differ: some seek long-term viability while activist funds may target short-term price movement.
options.B: Shareholders’ goals are irrelevant because boards must legally optimize only employee welfare in all cases.
options.C: Shareholders do not vote for directors because directors are appointed by auditors under SEC authority.
options.D: Shareholders are homogeneous because each share confers identical goals and identical time preferences.

2yr-20.stem: A public company’s stock price collapses; a bidder believes it can fix internal problems and launches a hostile bid. This illustrates:

options.A: The market for corporate control disciplining management when internal governance mechanisms have failed.
options.B: Adverse selection in hiring because candidates misrepresent capabilities during the recruitment process.
options.C: Long-tail dynamics because niche products accumulate into large revenues when marginal costs are low.
options.D: Bundling economics because negatively correlated products are sold together at discounted prices.

2yr-20.stem: In takeover contexts, ‘winner’s curse’ most accurately refers to situations where the acquirer:

options.A: Uses leverage to buy shares and take the company private, avoiding public disclosure obligations.
options.B: Adopts a poison pill that dilutes ownership once an acquirer crosses a threshold percentage.
options.C: Bundles two products with negatively correlated demand and sells them together at discount.
options.D: Pays a premium that results in overpayment and subsequent shareholder value destruction.

2yr-20.stem: Why have poison pills become rarer according to the chapter’s discussion?

options.A: SEC rules have fully banned poison pills for all listed companies since the global financial crisis.
options.B: Poison pills eliminate hostile bids perfectly, so acquirers stopped attempting takeovers altogether.
options.C: Actively involved institutional investors often oppose pills because they hinder efficient equity-market discipline.
options.D: Poison pills are now replaced by freemium pricing because digital services need user acquisition.

2yr-20.stem: Which act is illegal in the insider-information discussion, even though possessing insider information is part of an executive’s job?

options.A: Briefing the board about nonpublic operational setbacks during a confidential governance meeting.
options.B: Learning time-sensitive performance data before analysts see it in quarterly public filings.
options.C: Trading on material nonpublic information or tipping others who trade before public release.
options.D: Holding private internal data about production and demand trends as part of normal management work.

2yr-20.stem: A CEO uses corporate funds for extravagant personal perks that shareholders ultimately pay for. This is best described as:

options.A: Adverse selection, because the CEO misrepresented capabilities during recruitment for the role.
options.B: Thin markets, because only a few suppliers can provide luxury services to executives in time.
options.C: Long tail, because many small purchases aggregate into a large overall revenue distribution.
options.D: On-the-job consumption, a form of agency cost enabled by information asymmetry and weak monitoring.

2yr-20.stem: A firm discovers a senior hire cannot do key tasks, but effort is high. Which agency problem is most plausible?

options.A: Adverse selection, because the agent’s ability was misrepresented or misjudged before hiring.
options.B: Winner’s curse, because the firm overpaid for an acquisition due to bidding competition.
options.C: Moral hazard, because the agent can do the work but chooses to shirk effort after hiring.
options.D: Poison pill, because a defense provision triggered once an acquirer crossed ownership threshold.

2yr-20.stem: A scientist can complete assigned work but instead reallocates effort to a private project. Which is the best diagnosis?

options.A: Moral hazard, because the principal cannot easily verify best effort despite the agent’s capability.
options.B: Adverse selection, because the scientist’s skills were exaggerated during recruiting and screening.
options.C: Wholesale, because the firm sells through retailers at a fixed discount to recommended prices.
options.D: Short head, because the firm depends on a few blockbuster innovations rather than many small ones.

2yr-20.stem: A manager says: “Our new charging-fee policy is legal, so ethics is irrelevant.” Which correction is closest to the text?

options.A: If legal, the action is necessarily fair; markets enforce fairness automatically through customer choice.
options.B: Ethics equals compliance; therefore ethics analysis can be outsourced entirely to the legal department.
options.C: Legal actions can still be ethically questionable; ethics involves societal norms like fairness and reciprocity.
options.D: Ethics is only for nonprofits; for-profit firms optimize shareholder returns regardless of moral norms.

2yr-20.stem: Which action best illustrates ‘ethical pursuit of competitive advantage’ as a foundation for long-run performance?

options.A: Designing growth targets that can be met legally while rewarding transparent reporting and safe problem solving.
options.B: Hiding risks in complex disclosures as long as GAAP is followed and penalties remain unlikely.
options.C: Driving short-term stock spikes through aggressive goal pressure even when legal ambiguity is exploited.
options.D: Replacing codes of conduct with performance bonuses to signal that results matter more than process.

2yr-20.stem: A carmaker sells the vehicle and then sells recurring software upgrades and service subscriptions. Which model best captures the upgrade logic?

options.A: Agency, because independent agents sell and take commissions while the producer controls the retail price.
options.B: Razor–razor blades, because the initial sale can stimulate ongoing purchases of complementary high-margin add-ons.
options.C: Wholesale, because dealers buy at discount and set retail prices independently to earn resale margins.
options.D: Bundling, because negatively correlated product demands are combined and sold at a discount.

2yr-20.stem: A company charges a monthly fee for access regardless of how much the service is used. Which business model is this?

options.A: Pay-as-you-go, because billing scales strictly with measured consumption volume in each period.
options.B: Subscription, because users pay for access during a term whether or not usage is high.
options.C: Ultra-low cost, because a stripped service is cheap and upgrades are sold at premium prices.
options.D: Freemium, because the basic tier is free while premium tiers monetize advanced capabilities.

2yr-20.stem: A firm bills only per kWh consumed at charging stations. Which model fits best?

options.A: Pay-as-you-go, because the user pays only for the measured consumption of the service.
options.B: Subscription, because the user buys access for a time period regardless of actual consumption.
options.C: Agency, because commissions are paid to intermediaries who sell at controlled retail prices.
options.D: Wholesale, because retailers earn a margin over fixed discounts from recommended retail prices.

2yr-20.stem: Which bundling condition is most essential in the chapter’s example of the Office suite?

options.A: Supply is scarce so bundling reduces inventory costs through physical shelf space optimization only.
options.B: Demand is negatively correlated so different users value different components more, enabling discount bundles.
options.C: Demand is random so bundling makes price discrimination impossible and therefore increases piracy.
options.D: Demand is perfectly correlated so every user values every component equally, maximizing willingness to pay.

2yr-20.stem: A platform sells millions of niche accessories that individually sell rarely, but collectively matter. This is best described as:

options.A: Long tail, where many low-volume items add up when shelf space and distribution costs approach zero.
options.B: Winner’s curse, where takeover premiums cause acquirers to destroy value after integration challenges.
options.C: Short head, where most revenue comes from a few blockbuster hits supported by large marketing budgets.
options.D: Moral hazard, where agents shirk effort because principals cannot observe effort after contracting.

2yr-20.stem: Which external mechanism most directly strengthens governance by standardizing disclosure and enabling outsider scrutiny?

options.A: Bundling, which increases customer willingness to pay by packaging negatively correlated products.
options.B: Freemium, which lowers adoption barriers by giving away basic features to attract users.
options.C: SEC filing requirements plus audits under GAAP, which enable analysts to examine standardized statements.
options.D: CEO-chair duality, which accelerates decision-making by unifying oversight and operational authority.

2yr-20.stem: An investment bank’s analysts rate their own client firms more favorably. The best interpretation is:

options.A: A demonstration that ethics is culture-specific and therefore cannot be evaluated across firms.
options.B: A proof that GAAP is ineffective because accounting standards allow any narrative to pass audits.
options.C: A conflict of interest that can bias external monitoring even when the information is publicly available.
options.D: A reason to increase inside directors because external monitors cannot ever be objective.

2yr-20.stem: A company shifts from selling boxed software to cloud access that reduces piracy by monitoring logins. Which model shift is most accurate?

options.A: A move toward wholesale distribution that lets retailers set price and profit from resale margins.
options.B: A move toward a poison-pill defense that deters hostile acquirers by diluting their ownership stake.
options.C: A move toward long-tail selling that earns most revenue from niche items rather than popular hits.
options.D: A move toward subscription and cloud delivery that alters revenue timing and reduces piracy through monitoring.

2yr-20.stem: Which governance mechanism is most ‘internal’ according to the chapter’s phrasing about ethics and control?

options.A: Analyst coverage that reacts to quarterly filings and publishes buy/hold/sell recommendations.
options.B: An LBO that shifts ownership from public shareholders to private equity sponsors via leverage.
options.C: A poison pill that dilutes hostile bidders once they cross an ownership percentage threshold.
options.D: Business ethics embedded in culture and leadership cues that guide behavior beyond formal monitoring.

2yr-20.stem: Which statement best matches the board–CEO relationship described in the governance section for public companies?

options.A: The board reports to the CEO; the CEO approves budgets and appoints directors to monitor stakeholder issues.
options.B: The CEO reports to the board; the board approves budgets and oversees stakeholder issues and CEO performance.
options.C: The board replaces the CEO in daily operations; directors run units directly to reduce information asymmetry.
options.D: The CEO reports only to auditors; boards exist mainly to file SEC statements and manage disclosure timing.

2yr-20.stem: In Caselet C, which external governance mechanism is most directly at work?

options.A: Government regulators enforcing compliance obligations and penalties for violations of financial laws.
options.B: Bundling products with negatively correlated demand to increase willingness to pay across segments.
options.C: Stock options aligning manager incentives with shareholders through predetermined strike prices.
options.D: Inside directors increasing information flow to the board, reducing managerial opportunism directly.

2yr-20.stem: A compliance function is under-resourced because growth bonuses dominate. Which concept best diagnoses the systemic problem?

options.A: Long tail: many small compliance failures add up to a large revenue stream from niche customers.
options.B: Bad apple: a few employees broke rules, so replacing them is sufficient regardless of incentive design.
options.C: Thin markets: compliance staff and leadership cannot find each other to coordinate in time and space.
options.D: Bad barrel: the organizational climate and incentives normalize corner cutting beyond individual bad actors.

2yr-20.stem: An exchange operator knows far more than customers about custody risk but markets itself as ‘risk-free.’ This most directly reflects:

options.A: Bundling benefits that arise when products have negatively correlated demand across customer segments.
options.B: Poison-pill protection that deters hostile takeovers through share dilution at ownership thresholds.
options.C: Information asymmetry that can enable opportunism unless governance and ethics constrain claims.
options.D: Leveraged-buyout incentives that shift ownership to private equity through debt-financed share purchases.

2yr-20.stem: A compliance officer can do the work but chooses to underinvest effort because penalties will fall on the firm, not the individual. This is:

options.A: Winner’s curse, because overpayment for an acquisition destroys value after integration.
options.B: Moral hazard, because hidden effort and shifted costs increase incentives to shirk responsibility.
options.C: Adverse selection, because the officer misrepresented capability during hiring and screening.
options.D: Short head, because revenue depends primarily on a few blockbuster products, not niche variety.

2yr-20.stem: A manager says: “We complied with the letter of the law, so ethics is satisfied.” Which response best matches the chapter?

options.A: Ethics is an external audit function; therefore internal codes of conduct are unnecessary.
options.B: Ethics equals legal compliance; therefore ethical analysis is redundant once counsel signs off.
options.C: Law is a minimum standard; ethical evaluation can still judge actions questionable under societal norms.
options.D: Ethics is culture-relative only; therefore universal norms like honesty cannot guide business conduct.

2yr-20.stem: Which governance response most directly reduces information asymmetry between insiders and outsiders in a regulated financial platform?

options.A: Increasing CEO-chair duality to unify command and speed decisions in volatile markets.
options.B: Adding more inside directors only, to ensure the board receives richer internal operational updates.
options.C: Standardized public reporting plus independent auditing and regulator oversight of disclosures and controls.
options.D: Switching from pay-as-you-go fees to subscription pricing to stabilize revenue predictability.

2yr-20.stem: A platform charges fees per transaction; heavy users pay more, light users pay little. Which model is the best fit?

options.A: Bundling, because negatively correlated preferences allow discounting across multiple products.
options.B: Pay-as-you-go, because pricing scales with actual consumption of the service (transactions).
options.C: Subscription, because payment is tied to access over time regardless of usage intensity.
options.D: Wholesale, because intermediaries set final prices and profit from resale margins.

2yr-20.stem: A platform offers basic trading tools free, but charges for advanced analytics and priority support. Which model is closest?

options.A: Wholesale, because retailers set price and profit from a fixed discount to recommended price.
options.B: Ultra-low cost, because minimal service is cheap and upgrades are sold at premium a la carte.
options.C: Freemium, because a free base expands adoption while premium add-ons monetize power users.
options.D: Agency, because an intermediary sells at commission while the producer controls retail pricing.

2yr-20.stem: A crypto wallet app is free, but the firm earns margins on proprietary swaps and withdrawals. Which model is most precise?

options.A: Bundling, because multiple products with negatively correlated demand are sold together at discount.
options.B: Razor–razor blades, because the free core stimulates recurring purchases of profitable complements.
options.C: Poison pill, because discounted share purchases deter takeover attempts by diluting bidders.
options.D: Wholesale, because retailers buy at a discount and set their own final prices for consumers.

2yr-20.stem: Offering thousands of low-volume tokens while relying on search and recommendation to match niche demand is closest to:

options.A: Moral hazard, where agents shirk effort because principals cannot observe post-contract behavior.
options.B: Adverse selection, where candidates misrepresent ability during recruitment and screening.
options.C: Short head, where a few blockbuster tokens drive almost all revenues through mass marketing budgets.
options.D: Long tail, where many niche offerings aggregate into substantial revenue when marginal costs are low.

2yr-20.stem: Which statement best explains how digital platforms can overcome thin markets in niche assets?

options.A: They bundle negatively correlated products so each user buys more even if they want only one.
options.B: They centralize decision rights in a CEO-chair to speed governance and reduce dissent in oversight.
options.C: They deter hostile takeovers through poison pills that dilute acquirers beyond ownership thresholds.
options.D: They reduce transaction costs and search frictions so dispersed buyers and sellers can find each other.

2yr-20.stem: A public crypto firm’s shares fall sharply; activists accumulate stock and push for leadership change. Which mechanism is operating?

options.A: Board composition, where inside directors provide operational detail to help monitor management.
options.B: Business ethics, where values statements guide behavior beyond legal compliance requirements.
options.C: Executive compensation, where stock options align incentives by tying pay to future share prices.
options.D: Market for corporate control, where control contests discipline underperforming management.

2yr-20.stem: A firm adopts a poison pill. Which trade-off noted in the chapter helps explain why such defenses are controversial?

options.A: They deter bids and also eliminate winner’s curse, so acquisitions become value-creating by default.
options.B: They deter hostile bids but can hinder equity-market discipline, so institutional investors often oppose them.
options.C: They deter bids and also reduce SEC disclosure, so analysts cannot evaluate firms accurately anymore.
options.D: They deter bids and also create long tails, so niche products become the main revenue source.

2yr-20.stem: A private sponsor uses leverage to buy a listed exchange and take it private, aiming to restructure and later re-list. This is:

options.A: A leveraged buyout, which changes ownership from public to private using borrowed money.
options.B: A freemium model, where the basic service is free but premium features are paid add-ons.
options.C: A bundling model, where negatively correlated products are discounted when sold together.
options.D: An agency model, where a retailer sells on commission while the producer controls retail pricing.

2yr-20.stem: Which action is most clearly illegal under the insider-trading discussion in the governance section?

options.A: Trading securities based on material nonpublic information or tipping another trader before disclosure.
options.B: Discussing nonpublic risk controls with the board during confidential governance oversight meetings.
options.C: Collecting operational data faster than competitors through legitimate analytics and data infrastructure.
options.D: Learning internal transaction volume trends before they appear in the firm’s quarterly public reporting.

2yr-20.stem: A CEO’s lavish personal spending using company funds is best framed as which agency cost?

options.A: Winner’s curse because a takeover premium caused overpayment and post-deal value destruction.
options.B: Adverse selection because capability was unknown before appointment and screening was imperfect.
options.C: On-the-job consumption enabled by information asymmetry and weak monitoring controls.
options.D: Thin markets because few luxury suppliers exist, raising transaction costs and scarcity pricing.

2yr-20.stem: A firm issues a code of conduct but rewards rule-bending quietly. The chapter suggests employees will most likely:

options.A: Follow observed executive actions because informal culture and incentives outweigh slogans and duplicity is visible.
options.B: Ignore both because ethics is solely personal and cannot be shaped by organizational context.
options.C: Act ethically if and only if auditors explicitly test ethics adherence in annual financial statements.
options.D: Follow the written code because formal statements override daily rewards and punishments automatically.

2yr-20.stem: Which statement best represents business ethics as defined in the chapter?

options.A: A pricing policy that maximizes profit given customer willingness to pay in competitive markets.
options.B: A personal belief system that cannot be shared across cultures and therefore cannot guide firms.
options.C: An agreed-upon code of conduct in business grounded in societal norms, beyond legal minimums.
options.D: A set of SEC regulations specifying how firms must format disclosures under GAAP principles.

2yr-20.stem: A firm’s leadership sets revenue targets that can only be met by evading controls. The chapter suggests the most likely outcome is:

options.A: Higher ethical performance because intense goals always induce discipline and eliminate moral hazard.
options.B: Increased corner cutting and potential illegal behavior because top-down pressure and high stakes distort choices.
options.C: Lower information asymmetry because ambitious goals increase transparency through frequent reporting.
options.D: Lower short-termism because hard goals force leaders to focus on long horizons rather than quick wins.

2yr-20.stem: A business model is described as ‘strategy in action.’ Which statement is closest to the chapter’s meaning?

options.A: It replaces strategy because tactics and goals are identical once the firm selects a target segment.
options.B: It is the same as corporate governance because boards and auditors implement strategy directly.
options.C: It translates how to compete into a blueprint of tactics, target market, and monetization logic.
options.D: It is a takeover defense because it prevents hostile bidders from acquiring the firm cheaply.

2yr-20.stem: Which prompt in the business model framework most directly asks about value creation in economic terms?

options.A: Who are the stakeholders performing activities from suppliers through partners to customers?
options.B: How are activities linked and sequenced to create and deliver the offering at scale and quality?
options.C: What activities must be performed to create and deliver the offering reliably to customers?
options.D: Why does the model create value through its revenue streams and cost structure choices?

2yr-20.stem: A platform sells a few megahits and also many niche items using recommendation systems. The chapter implies it can:

options.A: Avoid thin markets only with poison pills, because takeover defenses create buyer-seller matching.
options.B: Earn only from the short head, because niche items cannot aggregate unless physical inventory exists.
options.C: Earn from short head plus long tail, because technology expands selection while still selling blockbusters.
options.D: Earn only from the long tail, because blockbusters disappear when recommendation engines are used.

2yr-20.stem: Which principle is most consistent with the MBA oath excerpt discussed in the ethics section?

options.A: Managers should maximize personal compensation as a proxy for shareholder value creation.
options.B: Managers should treat law and ethics as identical because only codified rules matter.
options.C: Managers should not advance personal interests at the expense of the enterprise or society.
options.D: Managers should avoid reporting risks to prevent panic and maintain market confidence.

2yr-20.stem: Which neglected business-model framework question most directly explains a compliance breakdown when KYC is outsourced to partners?

options.A: Who, because unclear stakeholder responsibility for core activities creates gaps in execution and accountability.
options.B: How, because process linkage is irrelevant if partner roles and accountability are not specified.
options.C: Why, because revenue and cost logic alone determines whether compliance controls are implemented effectively.
options.D: What, because listing activities is sufficient even if no party is accountable for performing them.

2yr-20.stem: Agency theory views the firm as a ‘nexus of legal contracts.’ Which implication is most consistent with that view?

options.A: Conflicts are addressed through incentives and monitoring embedded in contracts, with disputes often resolved legally.
