2yr-20.stem: In the chapter, a business model is defined most precisely as:

options.A: A governance charter that specifies director duties and audit requirements, while leaving customer value and pricing to markets, in practice.
options.B: A five-forces map that identifies entry, rivalry, substitutes, and bargaining power, while leaving revenue capture unspecified in practice, in practice.
options.C: A mission statement that describes values and purpose, while leaving tactics, target market, and revenue logic to emerge later, overall.
options.D: A blueprint that translates strategy into action by specifying tactics, target market, customer needs, and how the firm makes money.

2yr-20.explanation: The textbook defines business models as translating strategy into action: tactics and initiatives, target market and customer needs, and the revenue logic for making money. Mission, governance charters, and five forces are related but not the business model definition.

2yr-20.stem: In the business model framework (why–what–who–how), which pairing is most accurate?

options.A: Why: cost structure; Who: suppliers only; What: audit standards; How: analysts’ buy-hold-sell recommendations over time, overall, as stated here.
options.B: Why: product features; Who: regulators only; What: board committees; How: hostile takeover defenses such as poison pills in practice.
options.C: Why: legal compliance; Who: courts; What: penalties; How: prosecutions that substitute for business model design in practice, in practice.
options.D: Why: value proposition and rationale; Who: target customers and stakeholders; What: offerings; How: revenue and delivery logic, in practice.

2yr-20.explanation: The framework guides leaders to define rationale/value, offerings, customers, and execution/revenue logic. The other options misplace governance and compliance items into the business model framework.

2yr-20.stem: Nespresso is presented as an example of which business model logic on the course page?

options.A: Razor-and-blade (bait-and-hook), where a durable platform is sold near cost while high-margin consumables generate profits, overall, as stated here.
options.B: Wholesale, where retailers buy at a discount and set resale prices, earning margin mainly through inventory turnover in practice.
options.C: Freemium, where a free version attracts users and a premium tier monetizes power users through feature gating over time.
options.D: Pay-as-you-go, where usage is metered and customers pay only for consumption without lock-in or proprietary complements, as stated here.

2yr-20.explanation: The course page explicitly frames Nespresso as bait-and-hook: machines (bait) and proprietary pods (hook), reinforced by lock-in. That differs from freemium, wholesale, or usage-metered pay-as-you-go models.

2yr-20.stem: Country Delight is used on the course page to illustrate which primary business model advantage of subscription?

options.A: Higher supplier power, because subscriptions force farms to accept lower prices and therefore raise margins automatically over time.
options.B: Better demand forecasting that reduces spoilage and middlemen costs, improving unit economics in a perishable supply chain, overall.
options.C: Lower buyer power, because subscription customers cannot cancel without regulatory approval and therefore become captive in practice, overall.
options.D: Lower threat of entry, because subscriptions legally prevent competitors from offering similar products in the same market, overall.

2yr-20.explanation: The course page highlights subscription enabling forecasting and reduced spoilage, especially in perishables. Subscriptions do not legally block entry, nor do they make cancellation impossible; supplier power effects are not automatic.

2yr-20.stem: D‑Mart’s EDLC–EDLP model is described on the course page as relying most directly on:

options.A: Asset ownership and working-capital discipline that enable low costs and low prices, reinforced by limited SKUs and cash discounts, overall.
options.B: Poison pills and takeover defenses that enable low costs by stabilizing control, reinforced by premium pricing and exclusivity in practice.
options.C: Freemium sampling and viral loops that enable low customer acquisition costs, reinforced by network effects and referral incentives, in practice.
options.D: Long-tail assortment and infinite shelf space that enable low prices, reinforced by niche variety and algorithmic discovery over time, overall.

2yr-20.explanation: The course page notes ownership choices, limited SKUs, and fast supplier payments to secure discounts—classic EDLC/EDLP mechanics. The other options are software platform or takeover tools or long-tail logic, not D‑Mart’s described model.

2yr-20.stem: Bundling is described on the course page as especially powerful when:

options.A: Products are commodities, so bundling creates lock-in solely by raising the list price without changing willingness to pay over time.
options.B: Products are perishable, so bundling ensures forecasting accuracy and therefore eliminates spoilage without subscription commitments, overall, as described, in practice.
options.C: Products are perfect substitutes, so bundling reduces competition by eliminating choice and forcing single-product adoption in practice, as stated here.
options.D: Products are negatively correlated in demand, so the bundle’s perceived value can exceed the sum of parts for many customers.

2yr-20.explanation: The course page emphasizes bundling negatively correlated products to create a ‘walled garden’ where value exceeds parts. Substitutes, list-price inflation, or perishability are not the core mechanism described.

2yr-20.stem: The long tail concept is best summarized (as in the course page and textbook) as:

options.A: Selling large volumes of a few blockbuster items is feasible when technology lowers distribution costs, shrinking selection in practice, in practice.
options.B: Selling niche items depends mainly on takeover defenses, because acquisition threats force firms to focus on blockbusters in practice, in practice.
options.C: Selling niche items requires physical shelf space expansion, so long-tail success depends mainly on owning more retail real estate over time.
options.D: Selling small volumes of many niche items becomes feasible when technology lowers distribution and search costs, expanding selection, as stated here.

2yr-20.explanation: Long tail is ‘selling less of more’: digitization and search lower distribution frictions and enable niche demand to be served. It is not primarily about blockbusters, physical shelf space, or takeover defenses.

2yr-20.stem: Threadless (textbook) best illustrates which business model innovation mechanism?

options.A: Wholesale distribution that shifts inventory risk to retailers, reducing downside by requiring retailers to prepay for all designs in practice.
options.B: Freemium pricing that converts users into paying customers by locking premium designs behind a paywall and limiting access over time.
options.C: Poison-pill governance that prevents hostile takeovers, reducing downside by avoiding acquisition premiums and winner’s curse in practice, as stated here.
options.D: Crowdsourcing and wisdom of crowds across the value chain, reducing downside by producing only designs validated by the community, overall.

2yr-20.explanation: The textbook describes Threadless as crowdsourcing design, forecasting, and demand validation (‘I’d buy it’), producing only community-approved designs to reduce downside. The other options confuse business model innovation mechanisms.

2yr-20.stem: Which diagnosis best distinguishes ‘strategy’ from ‘business model’ in the chapter’s framing?

options.A: Strategy is ethics; the business model is legality; governance is marketing; so each operates in separate silos over time, overall.
options.B: Strategy is pricing tactics; the business model is industry structure; governance then sets customer value and product positioning in practice.
options.C: Strategy sets the goal-directed competitive approach; the business model specifies the tactics and revenue logic that operationalize it, in practice.
options.D: Strategy is the board’s job; the business model is the regulator’s job; managers only execute without discretion in practice, overall.

2yr-20.explanation: The chapter explicitly positions business models as ‘strategy in action’: translating strategic intent into concrete initiatives and revenue logic. The other options scramble the relationships.

2yr-20.stem: Dollar Shave Club is used in the chapter as evidence that disruptive advantage can come mainly from:

options.A: GAAP reporting differences that hide true costs, making disruption an accounting artifact rather than real value creation in practice.
options.B: Business model innovation that changes economics and distribution, even when underlying product technology is not radically new, in practice.
options.C: Takeover defenses that prevent incumbents from acquiring entrants, making disruption legally protected over time, in practice, as stated here.
options.D: Radical product technology that makes competitors obsolete, even when distribution and pricing remain unchanged in practice, as stated here.

2yr-20.explanation: The chapter highlights Dollar Shave Club as business model innovation disrupting an incumbent—changing how value is delivered and captured rather than relying on breakthrough blade technology.

2yr-20.stem: Which statement best captures why business models are ‘dynamic’ in the chapter?

options.A: Business models never change once chosen, because stability guarantees competitive advantage and adaptation signals strategic weakness in practice, in the scenario, overall.
options.B: Managers must adapt tactics, partners, and revenue logic as environments shift; a once-effective model can become obsolete over time, as stated here.
options.C: Business models change only through hostile takeovers, because acquisitions are the only mechanism that can alter how firms make money in practice.
options.D: Business models change only when regulators rewrite accounting rules, because revenue logic is determined by GAAP rather than by design choices, overall.

2yr-20.explanation: The chapter treats business models as evolving: changes in technology, competition, or customer behavior can require adaptation. They are not fixed, not determined solely by accounting, and not changed only via takeovers.

2yr-20.stem: A platform aggregator earns from ads and discovery, while a logistics-focused competitor earns from delivery fees and membership. This contrast best illustrates:

options.A: Different ethics codes, where one has values and the other lacks them, so economics follow automatically from moral superiority in practice, overall.
options.B: Different profit drivers within similar markets, where the ‘how’ of the business model differs even when the ‘what’ looks similar, in practice.
options.C: Different governance mechanisms, where one firm uses a poison pill and the other uses GAAP audits to create competitive advantage in practice.
options.D: Different industry structures, where one operates in monopoly and the other in perfect competition, so business models do not matter over time.

2yr-20.explanation: The course page contrasts aggregator vs logistics models (e.g., Zomato vs Swiggy) in profit drivers—how value is captured. That is a business model difference, not a governance or ethics label by itself.

2yr-20.stem: Which situation best illustrates ‘thin markets’ as a barrier to long-tail success?

options.A: Too many buyers exist in each niche, so matching is easy and technology therefore cannot add value in practice, in practice.
options.B: Too few regulators exist, so markets cannot function and business models must be replaced by legal enforcement in practice, in practice.
options.C: Too many suppliers exist, so supplier power collapses and firms must rely on takeover defenses rather than matching over time, overall.
options.D: Too few buyers and sellers exist in each niche, so matching is hard unless technology aggregates demand and supply across boundaries.

2yr-20.explanation: Thin markets arise when there are too few participants for efficient matching. Aggregation and search technology can help—central to long-tail viability.

2yr-20.stem: A firm combines subscription with an ecosystem bundle. Which risk is most consistent with the chapter’s emphasis on ‘strategy in action’?

options.A: Guaranteed takeover immunity, because bundled customers prevent hostile bidders from paying premiums and therefore stop corporate control markets in practice.
options.B: Guaranteed lock-in, because adding tactics always increases switching costs regardless of customer perception in practice, overall, as described, in practice.
options.C: Complexity without value creation, if added tactics increase costs and confusion without improving customer value or unit economics, in practice.
options.D: Guaranteed ethics, because bundling and subscription reduce incentives to misreport and therefore eliminate bad-barrel risks over time, as stated here.

2yr-20.explanation: The chapter treats business models as translating strategy into actionable economics; adding tactics can backfire if it adds complexity without improving value or margins. Lock-in, ethics, and takeover immunity are not automatic.

2yr-20.stem: A firm offers a free tier with ads and a paid tier with premium features (Item 15). Which label fits best?

options.A: Wholesale only, because free tiers are equivalent to bulk discounts given to retailers who then set resale prices in practice.
options.B: Freemium, because a free version acquires users while a paid version monetizes a subset through feature gating and convenience, overall.
options.C: Subscription only, because all recurring payments are subscriptions regardless of free tiers, ads, and conversion funnels in practice, in practice.
options.D: Razor-and-blade only, because all recurring revenue must come from consumables rather than from upgrades and service bundles in practice, overall.

2yr-20.explanation: A free tier plus paid upgrade is the canonical freemium structure. Subscription can be part of the paid tier, but the defining feature is the free-to-paid conversion funnel; wholesale and razor-and-blade are different logics.

2yr-20.stem: A firm offers a free tier with ads and a paid tier with premium features (Item 16). Which label fits best?

options.A: Freemium, because a free version acquires users while a paid version monetizes a subset through feature gating and convenience, overall.
options.B: Razor-and-blade only, because all recurring revenue must come from consumables rather than from upgrades and service bundles in practice, overall.
options.C: Subscription only, because all recurring payments are subscriptions regardless of free tiers, ads, and conversion funnels in practice, in practice.
